Part 3 · Classic algorithms · ~40 min

Lesson 12: Naive Bayes

Bayes' theorem as a classifier — the classic spam filter, built step by step.

By the end of this lesson you can

  • Turn Bayes' theorem into a classifier
  • Explain the naive independence assumption and its limits
  • Build a spam filter by hand with Laplace smoothing
  • Choose between Multinomial, Bernoulli and Gaussian Naive Bayes
Before you start

This lesson builds on:

  • Lesson 4: Probability & Statistics — Probabilities run from 0 to 1. Bayes' theorem turns $P(B\mid A)$ into $P(A\mid B)$. Mean and standard deviation summarise data; the z-score $(x-\mu)/\sigma$ standardises it.
  • Lesson 9: Evaluating Models — Accuracy can mislead. Precision $= TP/(TP+FP)$, recall $= TP/(TP+FN)$, and F1 balances them. Moving the threshold trades one for the other; ROC-AUC summarises all thresholds.

Where this fits: A second classic algorithm, built directly on Bayes' theorem. Fast and a great baseline, especially for text.

1.A classifier built from Bayes' theorem

In Lesson 4 you used Bayes' theorem to update a belief given evidence: a positive test changed the probability of disease. Naive Bayes turns that idea into a classifier. The "evidence" is the example's features; the "hypothesis" is the class.

It's one of the oldest and simplest ML methods — the classic spam filters of the early 2000s were Naive Bayes — and it's still useful today: it trains almost instantly, needs little data, and works surprisingly well on text. In this lesson you'll build a spam filter completely by hand.

2.Bayes' theorem for classification

We want the probability of each class $y$ given the features $\mathbf{x} = (x_1, \dots, x_d)$:

$$P(y \mid \mathbf{x}) = \frac{P(y)\;P(\mathbf{x} \mid y)}{P(\mathbf{x})}$$
  • $P(y)$ — the prior: how common the class is overall (e.g. 40% of emails are spam).
  • $P(\mathbf{x} \mid y)$ — the likelihood: how probable these features are for this class.
  • $P(\mathbf{x})$ — the evidence: the same for every class, so for comparing classes we can ignore it.

So the prediction is the class with the largest $P(y)\,P(\mathbf{x} \mid y)$. We can always divide by the sum over classes at the end to get proper probabilities.

3.The "naive" assumption

The hard part is $P(\mathbf{x} \mid y)$: the probability of a whole combination of features. An email has thousands of possible words, and we'll never see most combinations even once, so we can't count them.

Naive Bayes makes a bold simplification: assume the features are independent of each other, given the class. Then the joint probability is just a product (the multiplication rule from Lesson 4):

$$P(x_1, x_2, \dots, x_d \mid y) = P(x_1 \mid y)\,P(x_2 \mid y)\cdots P(x_d \mid y) = \prod_{j=1}^{d} P(x_j \mid y)$$

which gives the Naive Bayes classifier:

$$\hat{y} = \arg\max_{y}\; P(y)\prod_{j=1}^{d} P(x_j \mid y)$$

($\arg\max_y$ means "the value of $y$ that makes this largest"; $\prod$ means "multiply together", like $\sum$ means "add up".)

Why "naive"?

The assumption is usually false. In real emails, "free" and "money" tend to appear together — they're not independent. Naive Bayes ignores that. Yet it often classifies well anyway, because it only needs to get the ranking of classes right, not the exact probabilities. Its probability estimates, however, tend to be over-confident (too close to 0 or 1).

Step-by-step derivationFrom Bayes' theorem to the Naive Bayes rule
  1. $$P(y \mid \mathbf{x}) = \frac{P(y)\,P(\mathbf{x} \mid y)}{P(\mathbf{x})}$$

    Bayes' theorem for a class $y$ and features $\mathbf{x}$.

  2. $$\hat{y} = \arg\max_y\ P(y)\,P(\mathbf{x} \mid y)$$

    $P(\mathbf{x})$ is the same for every class, so it can't change which class wins.

  3. $$P(\mathbf{x} \mid y) = \prod_{j} P(x_j \mid y)$$

    The naive assumption: features independent given the class.

  4. $$\hat{y} = \arg\max_y\ P(y)\prod_{j} P(x_j \mid y)$$

    Substitute.

  5. $$\hat{y} = \arg\max_y\ \Big[\ln P(y) + \sum_j \ln P(x_j \mid y)\Big]$$

    Take logs: the logarithm only ever increases, so the winner is the same — and sums don't underflow.

Read the formulaThe Naive Bayes rule
$$\hat{y} = \htmlClass{fd-1}{\arg\max_y}\ \htmlClass{fd-2}{P(y)}\htmlClass{fd-3}{\prod_{j=1}^{d} P(x_j \mid y)}$$
  • argmax — pick the class with the highest score
  • P(y) — prior — how common the class is
  • Π P(xⱼ | y) — multiply the evidence from each feature (the naive independence assumption)

Hover over (or tap) a part to highlight it in the formula.

4.Worked example: a spam filter by hand

Our tiny training set: 10 emails, 4 spam and 6 not spam ("ham").

Spam (4)Ham (6)
win money nowmeeting at noon
free money offerlunch with the team now
win a free prize nowproject meeting notes
claim your free prizesee you at lunch
your project report is ready
notes from the team meeting

Task: is the new email "free money now" spam?

Step 1 — priors

$P(\text{spam}) = 4/10 = 0.4$, $\quad P(\text{ham}) = 6/10 = 0.6$.

Step 2 — word probabilities (likelihoods)

We treat each email as a "bag of words" and count how often each word appears in each class. The spam emails contain 15 words in total; the ham emails contain 25. There are 24 different words in the vocabulary overall.

The probability of a word given a class is its count divided by the total word count of that class. But there's a trap: "free" never appears in ham, so $P(\text{free} \mid \text{ham}) = 0/25 = 0$ — and since we multiply, a single zero would make the whole ham probability zero, no matter what the other words say. One unseen word shouldn't be able to veto everything.

Laplace (add-one) smoothing

Pretend every vocabulary word was seen once more than it really was:

$$P(w \mid y) = \frac{\text{count}(w, y) + 1}{\text{total words in } y + |V|}$$

where $|V|$ is the vocabulary size (24). This guarantees no probability is ever zero. (In scikit-learn this "+1" is the parameter alpha=1.0.)

WordCount in spamP(w | spam)Count in hamP(w | ham)
free3$\frac{3+1}{15+24} = \frac{4}{39} = 0.1026$0$\frac{0+1}{25+24} = \frac{1}{49} = 0.0204$
money2$\frac{3}{39} = 0.0769$0$\frac{1}{49} = 0.0204$
now2$\frac{3}{39} = 0.0769$1$\frac{2}{49} = 0.0408$

Step 3 — multiply

$$\text{spam score} = 0.4 \times 0.1026 \times 0.0769 \times 0.0769 \approx 0.000243$$ $$\text{ham score} = 0.6 \times 0.0204 \times 0.0204 \times 0.0408 \approx 0.0000102$$

Step 4 — normalise into probabilities

$$P(\text{spam} \mid \text{"free money now"}) = \frac{0.000243}{0.000243 + 0.0000102} \approx 0.96$$

96% spam. Notice how each word contributed: "free" is about 5× more likely in spam than ham, "money" about 3.8×, and "now" about 1.9× — together they overwhelm the prior, which favoured ham.

5.Working with logs

In plain wordsMultiplying many small probabilities gives numbers too small for a computer to store, so in practice we add their logarithms instead. The winning class stays the same.

A real email has hundreds of words. Multiplying hundreds of numbers like 0.001 gives results so small that computers round them to exactly 0 (underflow). The fix: take logarithms. Since $\ln(ab) = \ln a + \ln b$, products become sums:

$$\ln\!\Big(P(y)\prod_j P(x_j \mid y)\Big) = \ln P(y) + \sum_j \ln P(x_j \mid y)$$

The logarithm keeps the ordering (bigger stays bigger), so we can compare the log-scores directly. Every Naive Bayes implementation works this way.

Worked example — the same email in log space

Spam: $\ln 0.4 + \ln 0.1026 + \ln 0.0769 + \ln 0.0769 \approx -0.916 - 2.277 - 2.565 - 2.565 = -8.32$.

Ham: $\ln 0.6 + \ln 0.0204 + \ln 0.0204 + \ln 0.0408 \approx -0.511 - 3.892 - 3.892 - 3.199 = -11.49$.

Spam's log-score is higher (less negative) → predict spam. The difference, $-8.32 - (-11.49) = 3.17$, means spam is $e^{3.17} \approx 24$ times more likely, i.e. $24/25 = 0.96$. Same answer.

Make sense of it

The situation: A real spam filter multiplies hundreds of small probabilities. Computers can't store numbers that tiny, so they add logarithms instead.

What the result tells you: The log scores −8.32 (spam) and −11.49 (ham) differ by 3.17, so spam is $e^{3.17} \approx 24$ times more likely: a 96% chance.

What if…?

  • The email also says "meeting" (3 times in ham, never in spam): the chance of spam falls to 88%. One ham-like word pulls it back.
  • "free" appears twice: its evidence counts twice, and the chance rises to 99.2%.
  • Spam is rarer (prior 0.1 instead of 0.4): the same words now give 80%. The prior matters.
  • No smoothing: "free" has probability 0 in ham, the ham score is 0, and the email is 100% spam whatever else it says.

Why it matters in ML: Each word adds its own log-evidence for or against a class, so the model is easy to explain: you can list the words that pushed the decision. The "naive" independence assumption makes repeated or correlated words over-count.

Advanced · optionalNormalising log-scores safely: the log-sum-exp trick

To turn class log-scores $a_k$ into probabilities you need $P(k) = e^{a_k}/\sum_j e^{a_j}$, but $e^{a_k}$ underflows to 0 when $a_k$ is around −800. Subtract the largest score $m = \max_j a_j$ first:

$$\log\sum_j e^{a_j} = m + \log\sum_j e^{a_j - m}, \qquad P(k) = e^{\,a_k - m}\Big/\sum_j e^{a_j - m}.$$

Every exponent is now ≤ 0 and the largest is exactly $e^0 = 1$, so nothing overflows and the sum is at least 1. Example: scores $-1000$ and $-1001$ would both underflow, but after subtracting $m = -1000$ they become $0$ and $-1$, giving probabilities $1/(1+e^{-1}) \approx 0.731$ and $0.269$. The same trick sits inside every softmax in Lessons 18–19.

6.Try it: your own spam filter

This filter is trained on exactly the 10 emails above. Type any message and see the score each word contributes. Green bars push towards spam, purple bars towards ham; the bar length is $\ln\frac{P(w \mid \text{spam})}{P(w \mid \text{ham})}$. Words never seen in training are ignored. Try "win a free lunch", "team meeting now", or "claim your prize".

7.Variants for different kinds of features

In plain wordsDifferent kinds of features need different versions: word counts (Multinomial), yes/no features (Bernoulli) or measurements like height (Gaussian, which assumes a bell curve for each class).

The formula $P(y)\prod_j P(x_j \mid y)$ is always the same; what changes is how $P(x_j \mid y)$ is modelled.

VariantFeatures$P(x_j \mid y)$ comes fromTypical use
Multinomial NBCountsSmoothed relative frequencies (as above)Text classification
Bernoulli NBBinary (present / absent)Fraction of examples where the feature is 1Short texts, yes/no features
Gaussian NBContinuous numbersA normal distribution per class and featureMeasurements
Complement NBCountsStatistics from all other classesImbalanced text data
Categorical NBCategoriesSmoothed frequency of each categoryCategorical data

Gaussian Naive Bayes

For continuous features, assume each feature follows a normal distribution (Lesson 4) within each class, with its own mean $\mu_{y}$ and standard deviation $\sigma_{y}$ estimated from the training data:

$$P(x_j \mid y) = \frac{1}{\sigma_{y}\sqrt{2\pi}}\exp\!\left(-\frac{(x_j - \mu_{y})^2}{2\sigma_{y}^2}\right)$$
Worked example — apple or orange?

From training data: apples weigh on average $\mu = 150$ g ($\sigma = 20$); oranges $\mu = 200$ g ($\sigma = 25$). Equal priors (0.5 each). A fruit weighs 170 g.

Apple: $z = (170 - 150)/20 = 1$. Density $= \frac{1}{20\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-1^2/2} \approx 0.01995 \times 0.607 \approx 0.0121$.

Orange: $z = (170 - 200)/25 = -1.2$. Density $= \frac{1}{25\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-1.44/2} \approx 0.01596 \times 0.487 \approx 0.0078$.

$P(\text{apple} \mid 170\text{ g}) = \frac{0.5 \times 0.0121}{0.5 \times 0.0121 + 0.5 \times 0.0078} \approx 0.61$.

A 61% chance it's an apple — 170 g is closer to the apple average, measured in standard deviations. With more features (colour, diameter…) we'd multiply in more densities.

Make sense of it

The situation: A fruit-sorting machine on a conveyor belt weighs each fruit and must decide: apple or orange?

What the result tells you: 170 g is 1 standard deviation above the apple average but 1.2 below the orange average, so it's a bit more apple-like: 61%.

What if…?

  • 160 g: 80% apple. 175 g: 49% — almost a coin toss. 185 g: 25%. 200 g: 5%.
  • 80% of the fruit are apples (prior 0.8): a 170 g fruit becomes 86% apple, and even 185 g is 56% apple. A strong prior shifts the boundary.

Why it matters in ML: Gaussian Naive Bayes turns each feature into a likelihood using its mean and standard deviation, then multiplies. It trains instantly and gives probabilities — a good first baseline.

8.Strengths and weaknesses

StrengthsWeaknesses
Extremely fast to train: just countingThe independence assumption is usually false
Works with little data and many features (like text)Probabilities are often over-confident
Handles many classes naturallyCan't learn interactions between features
Easy to explain: each feature adds evidenceGaussian NB assumes bell-shaped features

Naive Bayes is an excellent baseline: quick to try, hard to break. If a more complex model can't beat it, the complexity isn't earning its keep.

9.In Python

The spam filter from this lesson, with scikit-learn. CountVectorizer turns each text into word counts:

from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import CountVectorizer
from sklearn.naive_bayes import MultinomialNB

spam = ["win money now", "free money offer", "win a free prize now", "claim your free prize"]
ham = ["meeting at noon", "lunch with the team now", "project meeting notes",
       "see you at lunch", "your project report is ready", "notes from the team meeting"]

vec = CountVectorizer(token_pattern=r"(?u)\b\w+\b")   # keep 1-letter words like "a"
X = vec.fit_transform(spam + ham)
y = [1] * 4 + [0] * 6                                   # 1 = spam, 0 = ham

nb = MultinomialNB(alpha=1.0).fit(X, y)                 # alpha=1 is Laplace smoothing
tests = ["free money now", "meeting notes for the team", "win lunch now"]
print(nb.predict_proba(vec.transform(tests)).round(3))  # columns: [P(ham), P(spam)]

Output:

[[0.04  0.96 ]
 [0.985 0.015]
 [0.335 0.665]]

The first row matches our hand calculation exactly: 96% spam. "win lunch now" is mixed — "win" points to spam, "lunch" to ham — giving 67% spam.

Gaussian NB on the wine dataset from Lesson 11:

from sklearn.datasets import load_wine
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.naive_bayes import GaussianNB

X, y = load_wine(return_X_y=True)
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.25, stratify=y, random_state=0)
print(round(GaussianNB().fit(X_train, y_train).score(X_test, y_test), 3))   # 0.956

95.6% accuracy with no scaling and no tuning, trained in milliseconds — better than kNN's 93.3% on the same split.

10.Running example: Chennai Homes

Naive Bayes on the listing text alone: words like "new" and "metro" push towards selling fast, "old" and "renovation" away. "New flat near metro" scores 0.96; "old villa needs renovation" just 0.02; "quiet flat with garden" is mixed (0.59).

Same 12 houses as Lesson 1. With so little data, treat the numbers as an illustration of the method, not as reliable estimates.

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
df = pd.read_csv("houses.csv")   # download it from Lesson 1
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import CountVectorizer
from sklearn.naive_bayes import MultinomialNB
vec = CountVectorizer()
Xw = vec.fit_transform(df["description"])
nb = MultinomialNB(alpha=1.0).fit(Xw, df["sold_fast"])
for text in ["new flat near metro", "old villa needs renovation", "quiet flat with garden"]:
    print(f"{text:28s} P(sells fast) = {nb.predict_proba(vec.transform([text]))[0, 1]:.2f}")

Output:

new flat near metro          P(sells fast) = 0.96
old villa needs renovation   P(sells fast) = 0.02
quiet flat with garden       P(sells fast) = 0.59

⇄ Compare side by side: Naive Bayes vs logistic regression

Where this is used
  • Spam and sentiment classification
  • Document categorisation
  • A very fast baseline for text

Choose it when: Text or many features, little data, and when speed matters.

Think twice when: Features strongly interact, or you need well-calibrated probabilities.

Misconceptions to unlearn

MythNaive Bayes needs the features to really be independent.

RealityIt often works well even when they aren't — it only needs the right class to score highest.

MythNaive Bayes probabilities are reliable confidence levels.

RealityThey tend to be pushed towards 0 and 1. Use them for ranking, not as exact confidence.

Responsible AI · Language models of who is "normal"

Text classifiers learn which words go with which label. Sap et al. (2019) found that tweets written in African-American English were far more likely to be labelled offensive by widely used toxicity datasets and the models trained on them. A spam or moderation filter can silence some groups more than others; test it on varied dialects and writing styles before trusting it.

11.Questions beginners often ask

If the independence assumption is wrong, why does it work?

Because classification only needs the correct class to score highest. Errors in the exact probabilities often don't change which class wins.

Which variant should I use?

Multinomial for word counts, Bernoulli for present/absent features, Gaussian for continuous measurements.

Is Naive Bayes still used today?

Yes — as a fast baseline, for text classification with little data, and wherever training must be nearly instant.

Common mistakes to avoid
  • Forgetting smoothing, so one unseen word sets a class's probability to zero.
  • Multiplying many raw probabilities instead of adding log-probabilities (underflow).
  • Trusting Naive Bayes probabilities as well-calibrated confidence levels.
Interview corner

Don't confuse

  • Generative vs discriminative models — Describe each class vs draw the line between them.
  • Prior vs likelihood vs posterior — Before, evidence, after.

Hidden questions — answer in your head first, then open.

Why is Naive Bayes called "naive", and why does it still work?

The trap: Thinking the assumption must hold for it to work.

It assumes features are independent given the class, which is rarely true (words like "free" and "prize" go together). It still classifies well because it only needs the right class to score highest, not accurate probabilities — the ranking often survives the wrong assumption.

Can you trust Naive Bayes probabilities?

The trap: Reporting them as calibrated.

Usually not. Counting correlated evidence several times pushes probabilities towards 0 or 1 — in Lesson 12, repeating "free" lifted the spam probability from 96% to 99.2%. Use it for ranking or decisions, and calibrate if you need probabilities.

A word never appeared in any ham email during training. What happens without smoothing?

The trap: Thinking one word can't matter much.

Its estimated probability in ham is 0, so the whole ham score is 0 and the email is classified as spam with certainty, whatever its other words say. Laplace (add-one) smoothing prevents this.

Why do implementations add log-probabilities instead of multiplying probabilities?

The trap: "It's just a convention."

Multiplying hundreds of small numbers underflows to 0 in floating point. Logs turn the product into a sum of moderate numbers, and the class ranking is unchanged because log is increasing.

All 6 hidden questions for this lesson →

12.Key takeaways

  • Naive Bayes picks the class maximising $P(y)\prod_j P(x_j \mid y)$ — Bayes' theorem plus an independence assumption.
  • The "naive" independence assumption is usually wrong, but the classifier often works well anyway.
  • Laplace smoothing (+1 counts) prevents a single unseen word from zeroing out a class.
  • Implementations add log-probabilities instead of multiplying, to avoid underflow.
  • Multinomial NB for word counts, Bernoulli for yes/no features, Gaussian for continuous measurements.

13.Check your understanding

1. What does the "naive" assumption say?

Conditional independence lets us multiply individual feature probabilities instead of modelling every combination.

2. Why is Laplace smoothing needed?

Without smoothing, one zero factor in the product wipes out all the other evidence.

3. A class has 20 words in total, the vocabulary has 30 words, and "deal" appears 4 times in the class. With add-one smoothing, $P(\text{deal} \mid \text{class})$ is…

$(4 + 1)/(20 + 30) = 5/50 = 0.1$.

4. Why do implementations add log-probabilities instead of multiplying probabilities?

Products of hundreds of small probabilities become too small to store. Logs turn them into sums of manageable numbers, without changing the ranking.

5. Which variant suits features like height and weight?

Continuous measurements are modelled with a normal (Gaussian) distribution per class.

Exercise 2By hand

Priors: spam 0.5, ham 0.5. $P(\text{cheap} \mid \text{spam}) = 0.2$, $P(\text{cheap} \mid \text{ham}) = 0.02$; $P(\text{meeting} \mid \text{spam}) = 0.01$, $P(\text{meeting} \mid \text{ham}) = 0.1$. Classify "cheap meeting".

Lesson 13: Decision Trees

Twenty questions for data: Gini impurity, entropy, information gain and pruning.

By the end of this lesson you can

  • Read and follow a decision tree to make a prediction
  • Compute Gini impurity, entropy and information gain by hand
  • Explain how the CART algorithm chooses splits
  • Control overfitting with depth limits and pruning
Before you start

This lesson builds on:

  • Lesson 5: Data, Features & Generalization — Always judge a model on data it hasn't seen: split into train / validation / test, or use k-fold cross-validation. Overfitting = low training error but high test error. Never let test data leak into training.
  • Lesson 9: Evaluating Models — Accuracy can mislead. Precision $= TP/(TP+FP)$, recall $= TP/(TP+FN)$, and F1 balances them. Moving the threshold trades one for the other; ROC-AUC summarises all thresholds.

Where this fits: A completely different kind of model — questions instead of equations. Trees are the building blocks of the ensembles in Lesson 14.

1.Twenty questions with data

Remember the game "twenty questions"? You find an object by asking yes/no questions — "Is it alive?", "Is it bigger than a cat?" — each one narrowing down the possibilities. A decision tree classifies data the same way: it asks a sequence of simple questions about the features, like "Is petal width ≤ 0.8 cm?", until it reaches an answer.

Trees are one of the most popular model families in practice. A single tree is easy to read and explain; combined into forests and boosted ensembles (Lesson 14), trees are often the strongest models available for tabular data — spreadsheets and databases.

2.Anatomy of a tree

  • The root node at the top holds all the training data and asks the first question.
  • Each internal node tests one feature against a threshold: "$x_j \le t$?". Yes goes left, no goes right.
  • Each leaf at the bottom gives a prediction: the majority class of the training examples that ended up there (or their average value, for regression).
  • The depth is the number of questions on the longest path from root to leaf.

Here is a real depth-2 tree trained by scikit-learn on the Iris flower dataset (3 species, 4 measurements):

|--- petal width (cm) <= 0.80
|   |--- class: 0              (setosa)
|--- petal width (cm) >  0.80
|   |--- petal width (cm) <= 1.75
|   |   |--- class: 1          (versicolor)
|   |--- petal width (cm) >  1.75
|   |   |--- class: 2          (virginica)

To classify a flower with petal width 1.2 cm: is $1.2 \le 0.8$? No → go right. Is $1.2 \le 1.75$? Yes → versicolor. Anyone can follow that — a big advantage when decisions must be explained.

What the tree does to the feature space

Each question cuts the space with a straight line parallel to an axis. The tree chops the space into rectangles (boxes, in more dimensions), and each box gets one prediction. So decision boundaries look like staircases made of horizontal and vertical segments. You'll see this in the demo.

3.How does a tree choose its questions? Impurity

Picture itSorting laundry: a pile of only white shirts is "pure" — you know exactly what to do with it. A pile of mixed colours is "impure". A decision tree keeps asking questions until its piles are as pure as possible.

A good question separates the classes: after splitting, each side should be as "pure" as possible — ideally containing just one class. We need a number that measures impurity. Let $p_k$ be the fraction of examples in a node that belong to class $k$.

Gini impurity — the probability of mislabelling a random example if you labelled it randomly according to the node's class mix:

$$G = \sum_k p_k(1 - p_k) = 1 - \sum_k p_k^2$$

Entropy — from information theory, the average number of yes/no questions (bits) needed to identify the class:

$$H = -\sum_k p_k \log_2 p_k$$

Both are 0 for a pure node and largest when classes are evenly mixed. For two classes the maximum Gini is 0.5 and the maximum entropy is 1 bit.

Worked example — impurity of a node

A node has 10 examples: 6 "yes", 4 "no". So $p_{\text{yes}} = 0.6$, $p_{\text{no}} = 0.4$.

Gini: $1 - (0.6^2 + 0.4^2) = 1 - (0.36 + 0.16) = 0.48$.

Entropy: $-(0.6\log_2 0.6 + 0.4\log_2 0.4) = -(0.6\times(-0.737) + 0.4\times(-1.322)) \approx 0.971$ bits.

A pure node (10 yes, 0 no): Gini $= 1 - 1^2 = 0$, entropy $= -1\cdot\log_2 1 = 0$.

Make sense of it

The situation: A bank sorts loan applicants into groups. A group where everyone repaid is easy to act on; a 50/50 group isn't. Impurity measures that mix.

What the result tells you: Gini 0.48 means: pick two people at random from this node and there's a 48% chance they have different labels. Entropy 0.971 bits says you'd need almost one yes/no question to learn the label.

What if…?

  • 5 yes, 5 no: Gini 0.5, entropy 1 bit — the worst possible mix for two classes.
  • 9 yes, 1 no: Gini 0.18, entropy 0.47 — nearly pure.
  • Three classes, equally mixed: Gini 0.667, entropy 1.585 bits — more classes, more uncertainty.

Why it matters in ML: A tree's whole job is to make its leaves pure. Impurity is the score it uses to choose every question it asks.

Read the formulaGini impurity
$$G = \htmlClass{fd-1}{\sum_k}\htmlClass{fd-2}{p_k}\htmlClass{fd-3}{(1 - p_k)}$$
  • Σₖ — add up over every class
  • pₖ — chance a random example in the node is class k
  • 1 − pₖ — chance a random label would then be wrong

Hover over (or tap) a part to highlight it in the formula.

4.Scoring a split: information gain

A split sends $n_L$ examples left and $n_R$ right. Its quality is the weighted impurity of the two children, weighted by how many examples each gets:

$$G_{\text{split}} = \frac{n_L}{n}\,G(\text{left}) + \frac{n_R}{n}\,G(\text{right})$$

The improvement over the parent is the impurity decrease — called information gain when using entropy:

$$\text{Gain} = G(\text{parent}) - G_{\text{split}}$$
Worked example — compare two candidate splits

Parent: 6 yes / 4 no, Gini 0.48 (from above).

Split A sends 4 examples left (4 yes, 0 no) and 6 right (2 yes, 4 no).

  • Left Gini $= 0$ (pure).
  • Right Gini $= 1 - \big((2/6)^2 + (4/6)^2\big) = 1 - (0.111 + 0.444) \approx 0.444$.
  • Weighted: $\frac{4}{10}\times0 + \frac{6}{10}\times0.444 \approx 0.267$. Gain $= 0.48 - 0.267 = 0.213$.

Split B sends 5 left (3 yes, 2 no) and 5 right (3 yes, 2 no).

  • Both children have the same 60/40 mix as the parent: Gini 0.48 each. Weighted: 0.48. Gain $= 0$.

Split B is useless — it doesn't separate anything. Split A wins. (With entropy, split A's information gain is $0.971 - 0.6\times0.918 \approx 0.420$ bits; the ranking is the same.)

Make sense of it

The situation: The tree has to pick its first question. Each candidate split divides the 10 applicants differently.

What the result tells you: Split A creates one perfectly pure group and cuts impurity from 0.48 to 0.267 — a gain of 0.213. Split B leaves both groups as mixed as before, so it's worthless.

What if…?

  • A perfect split (6 yes on one side, 4 no on the other): both children are pure and the gain is the full 0.48.
  • Peeling off one example (1 yes alone, 5 yes + 4 no together): a pure leaf, but the gain is only 0.036. Tiny pure leaves look tempting and help little — that's how deep trees overfit.

Why it matters in ML: Trees choose splits greedily, one at a time, by the biggest gain. Limiting depth or requiring a minimum number of samples per leaf stops them chasing tiny pure leaves.

Advanced · optionalWhy a split never increases weighted impurity

Gini impurity $G(\mathbf{p}) = 1 - \sum_k p_k^2$ and entropy $H(\mathbf{p}) = -\sum_k p_k\log_2 p_k$ are concave functions of the class proportions $\mathbf{p}$. A split sends a fraction $w_L$ of a node's examples left and $w_R = 1-w_L$ right, and the parent's proportions are the weighted average $\mathbf{p} = w_L\mathbf{p}_L + w_R\mathbf{p}_R$. Concavity (Jensen's inequality) gives

$$G(w_L\mathbf{p}_L + w_R\mathbf{p}_R) \;\ge\; w_L G(\mathbf{p}_L) + w_R G(\mathbf{p}_R),$$

so the information gain is always ≥ 0, and it is 0 only when both children have the same class mix as the parent. That's why a tree keeps finding "useful" splits all the way down to pure leaves — and why it must be stopped deliberately (Lesson 13's overfitting section).

5.Growing the tree: the CART algorithm

scikit-learn builds trees with an optimised version of CART (Classification And Regression Trees). It's greedy and recursive:

  1. At the current node, try every feature, and for each feature every possible threshold (the midpoints between sorted values).
  2. Pick the feature and threshold with the largest impurity decrease.
  3. Split the data into left and right children.
  4. Repeat on each child, until a stopping rule is met (node is pure, maximum depth reached, too few examples to split…).

"Greedy" means it picks the best split right now, without looking ahead. That's not guaranteed to find the best possible tree (that problem is far too hard to solve exactly), but it works very well in practice.

6.Try it: watch a tree carve up the space

The tree below is grown on the points using Gini impurity. Increase the maximum depth and watch it add axis-parallel cuts. At low depth it underfits; at high depth it carves tiny boxes around individual points — overfitting. The first few splits are listed underneath.

7.Trees for regression

For predicting numbers, a leaf predicts the average $y$ of its training examples, and impurity is measured by the variance (equivalently the MSE) within the node. A split is good if it creates groups whose $y$ values are tightly clustered. The result is a step function: flat predictions within each box, with jumps between boxes.

8.Trees overfit easily — and how to stop them

In plain wordsTrees keep splitting until they memorise the training data. Limit their depth or the minimum examples per leaf, or prune them after growing — and choose those settings with cross-validation.

Left alone, a tree keeps splitting until every leaf is pure — it can memorise the training set perfectly, noise included. Ways to control it (all are hyperparameters, chosen by cross-validation):

  • max_depth — limit the number of questions.
  • min_samples_split / min_samples_leaf — don't split tiny groups; every leaf must contain at least this many examples.
  • max_leaf_nodes — cap the total number of leaves.
  • Cost-complexity pruning (ccp_alpha) — grow a full tree, then cut back branches that don't earn their keep. It minimises
$$R_\alpha(T) = R(T) + \alpha\,|T|$$

where $R(T)$ is the tree's training error (impurity), $|T|$ is its number of leaves, and $\alpha$ charges a price per leaf — the same "fit + penalty" idea as regularization in Lesson 10.

9.Feature importance

Each split reduces impurity. Add up those reductions for each feature (weighted by the number of examples reaching the node) and normalise so they sum to 1: that's the tree's feature importance. It tells you which features the tree relied on most.

Read importances with care

Impurity-based importance favours features with many distinct values (like IDs or continuous measurements), and when two features are correlated, the tree may use just one, making the other look unimportant. It describes the model, not causation.

10.Strengths and weaknesses

StrengthsWeaknesses
Easy to read and explainOverfit easily without limits
No feature scaling needed — splits compare a feature with a threshold, so units don't matterUnstable: a small change in data can produce a very different tree (high variance)
Handles numeric and categorical features, non-linear patterns and interactionsBoundaries are axis-parallel staircases; a diagonal boundary needs many steps
Fast to train and predictA single tree is rarely the most accurate model

The instability problem has a beautiful fix: train many trees and combine them. That's Lesson 14.

11.In Python

from sklearn.datasets import load_breast_cancer
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier

data = load_breast_cancer()
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    data.data, data.target, test_size=0.25, stratify=data.target, random_state=0)

for depth in [1, 2, 3, 5, None]:          # None = grow until leaves are pure
    tree = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=depth, random_state=0).fit(X_train, y_train)
    print(f"max_depth={str(depth):4s} depth={tree.get_depth()} leaves={tree.get_n_leaves():2d} "
          f"train={tree.score(X_train, y_train):.3f} test={tree.score(X_test, y_test):.3f}")

tree = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=3, random_state=0).fit(X_train, y_train)
top = sorted(zip(tree.feature_importances_, data.feature_names), reverse=True)[:3]
print([(str(name), round(float(imp), 3)) for imp, name in top])

Output:

max_depth=1    depth=1 leaves= 2 train=0.930 test=0.888
max_depth=2    depth=2 leaves= 4 train=0.932 test=0.888
max_depth=3    depth=3 leaves= 8 train=0.977 test=0.916
max_depth=5    depth=5 leaves=18 train=1.000 test=0.902
max_depth=None depth=5 leaves=18 train=1.000 test=0.902
[('worst perimeter', 0.791), ('worst concave points', 0.115), ('worst radius', 0.04)]

Depth 3 does best on unseen data (91.6%). Deeper trees reach 100% training accuracy but do worse on the test set — overfitting again. The depth-3 tree leans heavily on one feature, "worst perimeter" (79% of the importance). Notice that a single tree (91.6%) is below logistic regression's ~96% on this data (Lesson 8) — Lesson 14 closes that gap.

Print any tree as text with sklearn.tree.export_text(tree, feature_names=...), or draw it with sklearn.tree.plot_tree.

12.Running example: Chennai Homes

A depth-2 tree finds a simple rule: houses within 11.5 km and no older than 16 years sold fast. It fits all 12 training houses perfectly — which, with this little data, is more likely luck than proof (Lesson 5).

Same 12 houses as Lesson 1. With so little data, treat the numbers as an illustration of the method, not as reliable estimates.

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
df = pd.read_csv("houses.csv")   # download it from Lesson 1
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier, export_text
cols = ["size_m2", "dist_km", "age_yrs"]
tree = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=2, random_state=0).fit(df[cols], df["sold_fast"])
print(export_text(tree, feature_names=cols))
print("training accuracy:", tree.score(df[cols], df["sold_fast"]))

Output:

|--- dist_km <= 11.50
|   |--- age_yrs <= 16.00
|   |   |--- class: 1
|   |--- age_yrs >  16.00
|   |   |--- class: 0
|--- dist_km >  11.50
|   |--- class: 0

training accuracy: 1.0
Where this is used
  • Business rules that must be explainable (e.g. eligibility decisions)
  • Quick exploration of which features matter
  • The building block of random forests and boosting

Choose it when: You need a readable model, or features are a mix of numbers and categories.

Think twice when: You need top accuracy from a single model — use an ensemble instead.

Misconceptions to unlearn

MythFeature importance shows which features cause the outcome.

RealityIt shows what the tree used for splitting — biased towards features with many values, and silent about correlated alternatives.

MythA deeper tree is a better tree.

RealityDeeper trees fit training data better but overfit; depth must be tuned.

Responsible AI · Transparent, but not automatically fair

A small tree's rules can be read and audited, which is a real advantage for accountability. But readable is not the same as fair: a split on a proxy feature (such as a postcode) can encode discrimination plainly in the rules. Audit the splits, not just the accuracy.

13.Questions beginners often ask

Gini or entropy?

They usually give very similar trees. Gini is scikit-learn's default and slightly faster to compute.

Why don't trees need scaling?

Each split compares one feature with a threshold, so changing a feature's units just changes the threshold.

How deep should a tree be?

Choose max_depth (or min_samples_leaf) by cross-validation; shallow trees for explanation, deeper ones inside ensembles.

Common mistakes to avoid
  • Letting trees grow without limits and trusting their 100% training accuracy.
  • Scaling features for trees (harmless, but unnecessary).
  • Reading impurity-based feature importance as causal, or as fair between correlated features.
Interview corner

Don't confuse

  • Gini impurity vs entropy — Two rulers for the same mess.
  • Pre-pruning vs post-pruning — Stop early vs trim afterwards.
  • Impurity importance vs permutation importance — Credit claimed in training vs damage done when removed.

Hidden questions — answer in your head first, then open.

Do decision trees need feature scaling?

The trap: Scaling everything by habit.

No. A split asks "is $x \le t$?", and rescaling $x$ just rescales $t$; the tree is identical. The same goes for random forests and gradient-boosted trees.

A regression tree is trained on $x = 0, \dots, 9$ with $y = 2x$. What does it predict for $x = 100$?

The trap: Expecting 200.

18 — the value of the last leaf. Trees predict constants inside regions, so they can't extrapolate beyond the training range. Random forests and boosted trees share this limitation; linear models don't.

Why do fully grown decision trees overfit?

The trap: "Trees are just bad."

Without limits a tree keeps splitting until every leaf is pure, often isolating single noisy examples. Limit depth or leaf size, prune, or average many trees (a random forest).

Gini or entropy — does the choice matter much?

The trap: Spending a long time tuning it.

Rarely. They rank splits almost identically (in Lesson 13's example both preferred split A). Gini is slightly faster to compute. Depth and leaf-size limits matter far more.

All 7 hidden questions for this lesson →

14.Key takeaways

  • A decision tree asks a sequence of "feature ≤ threshold?" questions; leaves hold predictions.
  • Splits are chosen to reduce impurity: Gini $1 - \sum p_k^2$ or entropy $-\sum p_k\log_2 p_k$.
  • The CART algorithm greedily picks the split with the largest impurity decrease, then repeats on each child.
  • Unrestricted trees overfit; control them with max_depth, min_samples_leaf or pruning (ccp_alpha).
  • Trees are readable and need no scaling, but are unstable — which ensembles fix.

15.Check your understanding

1. A node has 5 examples of class A and 5 of class B. What is its Gini impurity?

$1 - (0.5^2 + 0.5^2) = 1 - 0.5 = 0.5$ — the maximum for two classes.

2. Which split is better: one that creates two pure children, or one whose children have the same class mix as the parent?

Pure children have impurity 0 — the maximum possible gain. Keeping the parent's mix gives zero gain.

3. Why don't decision trees need feature scaling?

Rescaling a feature just rescales its thresholds; the same examples go left and right.

4. A tree has 100% training accuracy and 85% test accuracy. What would most likely help?

That gap is overfitting; restricting the tree's growth reduces variance.

5. What shape are a decision tree's decision boundaries?

Each split is "one feature ≤ threshold", a cut parallel to an axis. Together they make rectangles.

Part 3 · Classic algorithms · ~50 min

Lesson 14: Random Forests & Boosting

Combine many trees: bagging, random forests, AdaBoost and gradient boosting.

By the end of this lesson you can

  • Explain mathematically why combining diverse models reduces error
  • Describe bagging, bootstrap samples and out-of-bag evaluation
  • Explain how random forests decorrelate trees
  • Run AdaBoost and gradient boosting rounds by hand
Before you start

This lesson builds on:

  • Lesson 10: Overfitting, Regularization & Bias–Variance — Error = bias² + variance + noise. Regularization adds a penalty on weight size (L2 ridge shrinks weights; L1 lasso zeros some) to reduce variance; its strength is chosen by cross-validation.
  • Lesson 13: Decision Trees — A decision tree asks a sequence of 'feature ≤ threshold?' questions chosen to reduce impurity (Gini or entropy). Deep trees overfit and are unstable.

Where this fits: Combines many trees into some of the most accurate models available for tabular data — often the first thing professionals try.

1.The wisdom of crowds

In 1906, at a country fair, about 800 people guessed the weight of an ox. Individual guesses were all over the place — but their median was within 1% of the true weight. Many independent, imperfect opinions, combined, beat almost any single expert.

Ensemble methods apply this to models: train many models and combine their predictions. Lesson 13 showed that a single decision tree is unstable — small changes in data produce a different tree. Ensembles turn that weakness into a strength. Random forests and gradient boosting, the two families in this lesson, win a large share of real-world competitions on tabular data.

2.Why combining models works: the maths

Picture itAt a village fair, nobody guesses the ox's weight exactly, but the average of hundreds of guesses is remarkably close. Many imperfect models whose errors differ can be better together than any one of them.

In plain wordsIf many models make different mistakes, a majority vote is right far more often than any one of them — 25 models that are each right 60% of the time are right about 85% of the time together.

Suppose you have 25 classifiers, each correct 60% of the time, and — crucially — they make their mistakes independently. You take a majority vote. The vote is right whenever at least 13 of the 25 are right. Using the binomial distribution:

$$P(\text{majority correct}) = \sum_{k=13}^{25}\binom{25}{k}(0.6)^k(0.4)^{25-k} \approx 0.846$$

Twenty-five 60%-accurate models make an 85%-accurate committee. With 101 such models it rises to about 98%.

($\binom{25}{k}$, "25 choose $k$", counts the ways to pick which $k$ of the 25 models are right.)

The catch: independence

This only works if the models make different mistakes. Twenty-five copies of the same model all fail on the same examples, so voting gains nothing. The art of ensembles is making models that are individually good and diverse. Bagging and random forests create diversity through randomness; boosting creates it by making each model focus on the previous ones' errors.

For regression the effect is easy to see too: averaging $M$ predictions with independent errors divides the variance by $M$ — exactly the "variance" part of the bias–variance trade-off from Lesson 10.

3.Bagging: bootstrap aggregating

We only have one training set. How do we train many different trees? Bagging creates a new training set for each tree by bootstrap sampling: draw $n$ examples from the $n$ originals with replacement. Some examples appear twice or more, some not at all.

Worked example — how much of the data does each tree see?

The chance a particular example is not picked in one draw is $1 - \frac{1}{n}$. Over $n$ draws: $\left(1 - \frac{1}{n}\right)^n$. For large $n$ this approaches $e^{-1} \approx 0.368$.

So each bootstrap sample contains about $1 - 0.368 = 63.2\%$ of the distinct original examples. (For $n = 1000$: $1 - 0.999^{1000} \approx 0.632$.)

Make sense of it

The situation: A random forest trains each tree on a "bootstrap" sample: draw examples at random, with replacement, as many times as there are examples.

What the result tells you: Each tree sees about 63% of the distinct examples, some of them more than once. The other 37% are "out-of-bag" for that tree.

What if…?

  • Small data: with 10 examples, 65% are picked; with 3, 70%. It settles at 63.2% as $n$ grows.
  • The left-out 37% can test each tree for free — the out-of-bag score, a built-in validation estimate.

Why it matters in ML: Different samples make the trees different, so their mistakes partly cancel when they vote. That's how bagging reduces variance without needing more data.

The algorithm:

  1. For $m = 1, \dots, M$: draw a bootstrap sample and train a deep (low-bias, high-variance) tree on it.
  2. To predict: majority vote (classification) or average (regression) over the $M$ trees.

Out-of-bag (OOB) evaluation is a free bonus: each example was left out of about 37% of the trees, so we can predict it using only those trees and get a validation score without a separate validation set.

4.Random forests

Bagged trees are still quite similar: if one feature is very strong, every tree splits on it first. A random forest (Breiman, 2001) adds a second source of randomness: at each split, only a random subset of the features is considered. A common default for classification is $\sqrt{d}$ features out of $d$ (scikit-learn: max_features="sqrt").

This forces trees to use different features, making them less correlated — and the less correlated the trees, the more averaging helps.

SettingEffect
n_estimators (number of trees)More is better up to a plateau; more trees never cause overfitting, they just cost time.
max_featuresSmaller → more diverse trees but each is weaker.
max_depth, min_samples_leafTrees are usually grown deep; limiting them adds bias but can help on noisy data.
Why random forests are so popular

They work well "out of the box" with little tuning, need no feature scaling, handle many features, give feature importances, and are hard to badly overfit. They're an excellent default for tabular data.

5.Boosting: learning from mistakes

Bagging trains models in parallel, independently. Boosting trains them in sequence: each new model focuses on what the ensemble so far gets wrong. It typically uses weak, shallow trees (even depth-1 "stumps") and combines them into a strong model. Bagging mainly reduces variance; boosting mainly reduces bias.

Analogy

A student preparing for an exam does a practice test, then spends the next study session on the questions they got wrong, then retests, and repeats. Each session adds a little knowledge targeted at the remaining weaknesses.

6.AdaBoost

In plain wordsAdaBoost trains models one after another; after each round, the examples it got wrong count more, so the next model focuses on them. Better models get a bigger vote.

AdaBoost (adaptive boosting) gives every training example a weight, starting equal. Each round:

  1. Train a weak learner on the weighted data. Compute its weighted error rate $\varepsilon$.
  2. Give it a vote of strength $\alpha = \frac{1}{2}\ln\frac{1 - \varepsilon}{\varepsilon}$ — accurate learners get louder voices.
  3. Increase the weights of misclassified examples (multiply by $e^{\alpha}$) and decrease the correct ones (multiply by $e^{-\alpha}$), then renormalise so weights sum to 1.

Final prediction: the $\alpha$-weighted vote of all learners.

Worked example — one AdaBoost round

10 examples, each weight 0.1. A stump misclassifies 3 of them: $\varepsilon = 0.3$.

Vote strength: $\alpha = \frac12\ln\frac{0.7}{0.3} = \frac12\ln 2.333 \approx 0.424$.

Wrong examples: $0.1\times e^{0.424} \approx 0.1\times1.528 = 0.153$. Correct ones: $0.1\times e^{-0.424} \approx 0.065$.

Sum: $3\times0.153 + 7\times0.065 \approx 0.917$. After dividing by it: wrong examples weigh about $0.167$ each, correct ones about $0.071$.

The 3 mistakes now hold 50% of the total weight (up from 30%). The next stump is forced to pay attention to them.

Make sense of it

The situation: A teacher sets the next practice test using the questions the class got wrong last time. AdaBoost does the same with its training examples.

What the result tells you: The stump is 70% right, so it gets a vote of 0.424. Then the 3 mistakes are up-weighted until they hold exactly half of the total weight.

What if…?

  • A better stump ($\varepsilon = 0.1$): its vote is 1.10, and again its mistakes end up with exactly 50% of the weight. This always happens: after each round, the last stump is no better than a coin toss on the new weights.
  • A coin-flip stump ($\varepsilon = 0.5$): its vote is 0 — it's ignored.
  • Worse than chance ($\varepsilon = 0.6$): its vote is negative (−0.20), so its predictions are flipped.

Why it matters in ML: Boosting focuses each new model on what the ensemble still gets wrong. That's powerful, but it also means noisy or mislabelled examples get more and more weight — boosting is sensitive to label noise.

7.Gradient boosting

Gradient boosting (Friedman, 2001) is the most widely used form today. The idea for regression with squared error is wonderfully simple:

  1. Start with a constant prediction $F_0(x) = \bar{y}$ (the mean).
  2. Compute the residuals — what's still wrong: $r_i = y_i - F_{m-1}(x_i)$.
  3. Fit a small tree $h_m$ to predict those residuals.
  4. Add it in, scaled by a learning rate $\eta$ (e.g. 0.1): $F_m(x) = F_{m-1}(x) + \eta\,h_m(x)$.
  5. Repeat for $M$ rounds.

Why "gradient"? For squared loss $\frac12(y - F)^2$, the negative gradient with respect to the prediction $F$ is exactly the residual $y - F$. So each tree takes a step of gradient descent (Lesson 7) — not in the space of weights, but in the space of predictions. Swapping in a different loss (log loss for classification, absolute error for robustness) gives a different "residual" to fit; the algorithm stays the same.

Worked example — two rounds by hand

Data: $x = 1, 2, 3$ with $y = 3, 5, 8$. Learning rate $\eta = 0.5$ (large, so the effect is visible).

Round 0: $F_0 = \bar{y} = 16/3 \approx 5.33$ for everyone. Residuals: $-2.33, -0.33, 2.67$. MSE $\approx 4.22$.

Round 1: fit a stump to the residuals. The best split is $x \le 2.5$: the left leaf predicts the mean residual of the first two, $(-2.33 - 0.33)/2 = -1.33$; the right leaf predicts $2.67$.

Update: $F_1 = 5.33 + 0.5\times(-1.33) = 4.67$ for $x = 1, 2$, and $5.33 + 0.5\times2.67 = 6.67$ for $x = 3$.

New residuals: $3 - 4.67 = -1.67$, $5 - 4.67 = 0.33$, $8 - 6.67 = 1.33$. MSE drops from 4.22 to $\approx 1.56$.

Round 2 fits a new stump to these new residuals, and so on. Each round fixes part of what's left.

Make sense of it

The situation: Predicting delivery times. The first guess is the average; each new small tree corrects part of what's still wrong.

What the result tells you: After one round the MSE falls from 4.22 to 1.56. Each tree predicts the residuals — the leftover errors — and only half its correction is applied.

What if…?

  • A third round (η = 0.5): MSE 0.20.
  • η = 1 (full corrections): MSE 0.67 after one round and 0.17 after two — faster, but with real noisy data this memorises the training set.
  • η = 0.1: after 10 rounds the MSE is still 0.85. Small steps need many trees, but generalise better.

Why it matters in ML: The learning rate and the number of trees work together: smaller steps plus more trees usually give the best test accuracy. Libraries like XGBoost and LightGBM use early stopping on a validation set to choose when to stop.

The learning rate and number of trees trade off: a small $\eta$ (0.01–0.1) with many trees generalises better than a large $\eta$ with few. Unlike random forests, boosting can overfit with too many rounds, so the number of trees is tuned — often with early stopping on a validation set.

Step-by-step derivationWhy each tree fits the residuals
  1. $$\ell = \tfrac{1}{2}\,(y - F)^2$$

    Squared loss for one example, where $F$ is the ensemble's current prediction.

  2. $$\frac{\partial \ell}{\partial F} = -(y - F)$$

    Differentiate with respect to the prediction (chain rule; the $\frac12$ cancels the 2).

  3. $$-\frac{\partial \ell}{\partial F} = y - F = r$$

    The negative gradient is exactly the residual.

  4. $$F \leftarrow F - \eta\frac{\partial \ell}{\partial F} = F + \eta\,r$$

    A gradient descent step on the prediction itself.

  5. $$F_m(x) = F_{m-1}(x) + \eta\,h_m(x)$$

    We can't adjust predictions point by point for unseen data, so a small tree $h_m$ learns to approximate the residuals $r$ as a function of $x$.

Advanced · optionalGradient boosting is gradient descent in function space

Think of the predictions $F(x_1),\dots,F(x_n)$ as the parameters. For the loss $L = \sum_i \tfrac12(y_i - F(x_i))^2$ the gradient with respect to each prediction is

$$\frac{\partial L}{\partial F(x_i)} = -(y_i - F(x_i)),$$

so the residuals are exactly the negative gradient. Fitting a small tree $h$ to the residuals and updating $F \leftarrow F + \eta h$ is one gradient-descent step, with the tree generalising the step to new points. For any other differentiable loss, boosting fits trees to the pseudo-residuals $-\partial L/\partial F(x_i)$: for log loss these are $y_i - p_i$, which is how gradient-boosted classifiers work. XGBoost goes one step further and also uses the second derivatives (a Newton step).

Read the formulaOne gradient boosting round
$$\htmlClass{fd-1}{F_m(x)} = \htmlClass{fd-2}{F_{m-1}(x)} + \htmlClass{fd-3}{\eta}\,\htmlClass{fd-4}{h_m(x)}$$
  • Fₘ(x) — the ensemble after round m
  • Fₘ₋₁(x) — the ensemble so far
  • η — learning rate — take only part of each correction
  • hₘ(x) — a small tree trained on the residuals

Hover over (or tap) a part to highlight it in the formula.

8.Try it: gradient boosting, tree by tree

Gradient boosting with depth-1 trees (stumps) fits the blue points. Add trees one at a time and watch the green prediction become a better and better step-shaped fit. The bottom panel shows the residuals the next tree will try to fit. Try a large learning rate, then a small one with many trees.

9.Modern boosting libraries

In plain wordsXGBoost, LightGBM and CatBoost are fast, polished versions of gradient boosting used widely in industry.

XGBoost, LightGBM and CatBoost are highly optimised gradient-boosting libraries. XGBoost, for example, adds regularization of the trees directly into its objective:

$$\text{obj} = \sum_i \ell(y_i, \hat{y}_i) + \sum_k \Omega(f_k), \qquad \Omega(f) = \gamma T + \tfrac{1}{2}\lambda\sum_j w_j^2$$

where $T$ is the number of leaves in a tree and $w_j$ are its leaf values — penalising both big trees and extreme predictions. scikit-learn's HistGradientBoostingClassifier uses a similar fast approach: it bins each feature into at most 255 bins, handles missing values natively, and turns on early stopping automatically for datasets with more than 10,000 samples.

10.Bagging vs boosting at a glance

Random forest (bagging)Gradient boosting
Trees trainedIndependently, in parallelSequentially, each fixing the last
Individual treesDeep (low bias, high variance)Shallow (high bias, low variance)
Mainly reducesVarianceBias
Overfits with more trees?NoYes — tune the number of trees
Tuning effortLowModerate (learning rate, trees, depth)
Typical accuracy on tabular dataVery goodOften the best

11.In Python

from sklearn.datasets import load_breast_cancer
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier
from sklearn.ensemble import (RandomForestClassifier, AdaBoostClassifier,
                              GradientBoostingClassifier, HistGradientBoostingClassifier)

X, y = load_breast_cancer(return_X_y=True)
models = {
    "single tree": DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=0),
    "random forest": RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=300, random_state=0),
    "AdaBoost": AdaBoostClassifier(n_estimators=200, random_state=0),
    "gradient boosting": GradientBoostingClassifier(random_state=0),
    "hist. gradient boosting": HistGradientBoostingClassifier(random_state=0),
}
for name, model in models.items():
    s = cross_val_score(model, X, y, cv=5)
    print(f"{name:24s} {s.mean():.3f} ± {s.std():.3f}")

rf = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=300, oob_score=True, random_state=0).fit(X, y)
print("out-of-bag accuracy:", round(rf.oob_score_, 3))

Output:

single tree              0.917 ± 0.016
random forest            0.963 ± 0.022
AdaBoost                 0.977 ± 0.009
gradient boosting        0.963 ± 0.021
hist. gradient boosting  0.965 ± 0.018
out-of-bag accuracy: 0.965

Every ensemble beats the single tree by 5–6 percentage points, with default settings. Notice the out-of-bag accuracy (0.965) closely matches the cross-validated score (0.963) — a free and reliable estimate. On this particular dataset AdaBoost edges ahead; on another dataset the order could differ, which is why we compare with cross-validation.

12.Running example: Chennai Homes

With 12 houses, leave-one-out accuracy is very noisy: a single tree scores 0.50, a random forest 0.58. The forest spreads importance across age, distance and size rather than relying on one split.

Same 12 houses as Lesson 1. With so little data, treat the numbers as an illustration of the method, not as reliable estimates.

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
df = pd.read_csv("houses.csv")   # download it from Lesson 1
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score, LeaveOneOut
cols = ["size_m2", "bedrooms", "dist_km", "age_yrs"]
for name, m in [("single tree", DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=0)),
                ("random forest", RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=300, random_state=0))]:
    acc = cross_val_score(m, df[cols], df["sold_fast"], cv=LeaveOneOut()).mean()
    print(f"{name:14s} leave-one-out accuracy {acc:.2f}")
rf = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=300, random_state=0).fit(df[cols], df["sold_fast"])
print({c: round(float(v), 2) for c, v in zip(cols, rf.feature_importances_)})

Output:

single tree    leave-one-out accuracy 0.50
random forest  leave-one-out accuracy 0.58
{'size_m2': 0.27, 'bedrooms': 0.04, 'dist_km': 0.31, 'age_yrs': 0.37}

⇄ Compare side by side: Bagging vs boostingClassical machine learning vs deep learning

Where this is used
  • Fraud detection, credit risk, insurance pricing
  • Ranking search results
  • A very common choice in data-science competitions on tabular data

Choose it when: Tabular (spreadsheet-like) data — usually the strongest choice.

Think twice when: Images, audio and raw text, where deep learning is usually better.

Misconceptions to unlearn

MythMore trees in a random forest can cause overfitting.

RealityAdding trees to a random forest doesn't make it overfit — it only costs time. (Boosting is different: too many rounds can overfit.)

MythAn ensemble of weak models can't beat one strong model.

RealityCombining many diverse, decent models is one of the most reliable ways to get top accuracy on tabular data.

Responsible AI · Accuracy versus explainability

Forests and boosting are often more accurate than a single tree but much harder to explain. Post-hoc tools (feature importance, SHAP values, partial-dependence plots) help, but they describe the model approximately and can be misleading — permutation importance, for example, spreads credit unpredictably between correlated features. For high-stakes decisions, consider whether a slightly less accurate but interpretable model is the responsible choice.

13.Questions beginners often ask

Random forest or gradient boosting?

Random forests work well with almost no tuning. Gradient boosting is often slightly more accurate but needs its learning rate and number of trees tuned.

How many trees?

For random forests, hundreds is typical — more never overfits, it only costs time. For boosting, choose with early stopping or cross-validation.

Can I still interpret an ensemble?

Less directly than one tree, but feature importances and tools such as permutation importance and partial dependence plots help.

Common mistakes to avoid
  • Using too many boosting rounds with a large learning rate, which overfits.
  • Assuming more random-forest trees causes overfitting — it only costs time.
  • Ensembling near-identical models, which barely helps.
Interview corner

Don't confuse

  • Bagging vs boosting — Committee in parallel vs relay team in sequence.
  • AdaBoost vs gradient boosting — Re-weight the examples vs fit the leftovers.
  • Out-of-bag score vs validation score — Free built-in check vs a dedicated exam.

Hidden questions — answer in your head first, then open.

Does bagging reduce bias or variance? And boosting?

The trap: "Both reduce error" without saying how.

Bagging (random forests) mainly reduces variance by averaging many deep, overfit trees. Boosting mainly reduces bias by adding simple models that correct remaining errors.

Will a random forest overfit if you add more trees?

The trap: Treating trees like boosting rounds.

No. More trees make the average more stable; the test error levels off, it doesn't rise. Gradient boosting is different: more rounds can overfit, so use early stopping.

Why does a random forest choose a random subset of features at each split?

The trap: "For speed."

To decorrelate the trees. The variance of an average of $B$ trees is $\rho\sigma^2 + \frac{1-\rho}{B}\sigma^2$, where $\rho$ is their correlation. With $\rho = 0.5$ and 100 trees it's 0.505σ²; with $\rho = 0.1$ it's 0.109σ². Bootstrap samples alone leave trees too similar, because they all split on the strongest feature.

What is the out-of-bag score?

The trap: Not knowing about it.

Each tree skips about 37% of the examples. Predicting each example using only the trees that didn't see it gives a free validation estimate, without a separate hold-out set.

All 7 hidden questions for this lesson →

14.Key takeaways

  • Combining many diverse models reduces error — but only if their mistakes are not all the same.
  • Bagging trains models on bootstrap samples (~63% of the data each) and averages them, reducing variance.
  • Random forests also pick a random subset of features at each split, making trees more diverse.
  • Boosting trains models in sequence; AdaBoost re-weights mistakes, gradient boosting fits each new tree to the residuals (the negative gradient).
  • Boosting needs the learning rate and number of trees tuned; random forests work well with little tuning.

15.Check your understanding

1. Why does a majority vote of many classifiers help?

If models err on different examples, the majority is usually right even when individuals are wrong.

2. What fraction of distinct examples does a bootstrap sample contain, roughly?

$1 - (1 - 1/n)^n \approx 1 - e^{-1} \approx 0.632$.

3. What does a random forest add on top of bagging?

Feature subsampling decorrelates the trees, making the average stronger.

4. In gradient boosting with squared error, each new tree is trained to predict…

The residual is the negative gradient of the squared loss; fitting it is a gradient descent step in prediction space.

5. A weak learner has weighted error $\varepsilon = 0.5$. What is its AdaBoost vote $\alpha$?

$\alpha = \frac12\ln\frac{0.5}{0.5} = \frac12\ln 1 = 0$. A coin-flip learner gets no say.
