Part 5 · Neural networks & real projects · ~70 min

Lesson 18: Neural Networks from Scratch

Neurons, layers, activations and backpropagation — built by hand in NumPy.

By the end of this lesson you can

  • Explain neurons, layers and why activation functions are needed
  • Run a forward pass through a small network by hand
  • Run backpropagation by hand and update the weights
  • Implement and train a neural network from scratch in NumPy
Before you start

This lesson builds on:

  • Lesson 3: Derivatives & Gradients — A derivative is a slope; the gradient $\nabla L$ collects all partial derivatives and points uphill. Gradient descent steps the other way: $\mathbf{w} \leftarrow \mathbf{w} - \eta\nabla L$. The chain rule differentiates functions inside functions.
  • Lesson 7: Gradient Descent — Gradient descent trains almost any model: compute the gradient of the loss, step against it, repeat. The learning rate controls the step size; too large diverges. Mini-batches make it fast on big data.
  • Lesson 8: Logistic Regression — Logistic regression outputs a probability $p = \sigma(\mathbf{w}\cdot\mathbf{x} + b)$, is trained with log loss, and classifies with a threshold (often 0.5), giving a straight decision boundary.

Where this fits: Starts Part 5. Neural networks combine everything so far — dot products, activations like the sigmoid, losses, the chain rule and gradient descent.

1.Why neural networks?

Every model so far has a fixed shape: a straight line, a set of boxes, a kernel. Neural networks learn their own internal features. Stack enough simple units together and the network can represent extremely complicated relationships — recognising faces, translating languages, generating text. Modern AI is built on them.

The good news: you already know every ingredient. A neuron is logistic regression (Lesson 8). Training is gradient descent (Lesson 7). And the famous backpropagation algorithm is the chain rule (Lesson 3), applied carefully. In this lesson you'll compute a full forward and backward pass by hand, then write a working network in about 20 lines of NumPy.

2.The artificial neuron

Picture itDeciding whether to go for a run, you weigh the weather, how tired you are and whether a friend is coming, then decide yes or no. A neuron does the same: weigh the inputs, add them up, and squash the total into a decision.

A neuron takes inputs $x_1, \dots, x_d$, multiplies each by a weight, adds a bias, and passes the result through an activation function $g$:

$$z = \mathbf{w}\cdot\mathbf{x} + b, \qquad a = g(z)$$

With $g = $ sigmoid, a single neuron is logistic regression. It draws one straight boundary. To learn more complex shapes, we connect many neurons in layers.

Loosely inspired by the brain

A biological neuron receives signals from other neurons, and "fires" if the combined signal is strong enough. The artificial version is a very simplified mathematical cartoon of that: weighted inputs, summed, then squashed. Don't take the analogy too far — what matters is the maths.

Read the formulaOne neuron
$$\htmlClass{fd-1}{a} = \htmlClass{fd-2}{g}\big(\htmlClass{fd-3}{\mathbf{w}\cdot\mathbf{x}} + \htmlClass{fd-4}{b}\big)$$
  • a — the neuron's output (activation)
  • g — activation function, e.g. ReLU — adds the non-linearity
  • w · x — weighted sum of the inputs
  • b — bias — shifts the threshold

Hover over (or tap) a part to highlight it in the formula.

3.Why one neuron isn't enough: XOR

The XOR ("exclusive or") function outputs 1 when exactly one input is 1:

x1x2XOR
000
011
101
110

Plot the four points: the 1s sit on one diagonal, the 0s on the other. No single straight line separates them, so no single neuron (and no logistic regression) can learn XOR. But two neurons can each draw one line, and a third neuron can combine their answers — "above line A and below line B". That's the power of hidden layers: they create new features that make the problem easy for the next layer.

4.Layers: the multilayer perceptron

A multilayer perceptron (MLP), or feed-forward network, has:

  • an input layer — the features (no computation);
  • one or more hidden layers — neurons whose outputs feed the next layer;
  • an output layer — the prediction.

Each layer does a matrix multiplication (Lesson 2) followed by an activation:

$$\mathbf{h} = g\big(W^{[1]}\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{b}^{[1]}\big), \qquad \hat{y} = \sigma\big(\mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{h} + c\big)$$

Here $W^{[1]}$ is a matrix with one row of weights per hidden neuron. With $d$ inputs and $m$ hidden neurons it has shape $m \times d$, plus $m$ biases.

Why activation functions are essential

Without $g$, two layers collapse into one: $V(W\mathbf{x}) = (VW)\mathbf{x}$, still a linear model. The non-linear activation is what lets depth add power.

5.Activation functions

NameFormulaRangeTypical use
ReLU$\max(0, z)$$[0, \infty)$Default for hidden layers
Sigmoid$\frac{1}{1 + e^{-z}}$$(0, 1)$Output for binary classification
tanh$\frac{e^z - e^{-z}}{e^z + e^{-z}}$$(-1, 1)$Hidden layers (zero-centred)
Softmax$\frac{e^{z_k}}{\sum_j e^{z_j}}$probabilities summing to 1Output for multi-class

Their derivatives, needed for training: ReLU′ is 1 if $z > 0$ else 0; $\sigma'(z) = \sigma(z)(1 - \sigma(z))$; $\tanh'(z) = 1 - \tanh^2(z)$. ReLU is popular because it's cheap and its gradient doesn't shrink for positive inputs, which helps deep networks train (Lesson 19).

6.Worked example: a forward pass

Worked example — a 2-2-1 network

Inputs $\mathbf{x} = (1, 0)$, true label $y = 1$. Two sigmoid hidden neurons, one sigmoid output, all biases 0.

Hidden weights: neuron 1 has $(0.5,\ 0.3)$, neuron 2 has $(-0.5,\ 0.8)$. Output weights $\mathbf{v} = (1,\ -1)$.

Hidden layer:
$z_1 = 0.5\cdot1 + 0.3\cdot0 = 0.5 \Rightarrow h_1 = \sigma(0.5) \approx 0.6225$
$z_2 = -0.5\cdot1 + 0.8\cdot0 = -0.5 \Rightarrow h_2 = \sigma(-0.5) \approx 0.3775$

Output: $z = 1\cdot0.6225 - 1\cdot0.3775 = 0.2449 \Rightarrow p = \sigma(0.2449) \approx 0.5609$.

Loss (log loss, Lesson 8): $L = -\ln 0.5609 \approx 0.578$. The network gives only a 56% chance to the correct answer. Let's teach it.

Make sense of it

The situation: A tiny network decides whether to approve something from two yes/no signals. Each hidden neuron is a small feature detector; the output neuron weighs their opinions.

What the result tells you: Neuron 1 likes input 1 (output 0.62); neuron 2 dislikes it (0.38). The output adds them with weights +1 and −1, giving 0.56 — barely leaning towards "yes".

What if…?

  • Other input $\mathbf{x} = (0, 1)$: the hidden outputs become 0.57 and 0.69, and $p$ drops to 0.47 — the network now leans "no" (loss 0.75 if the truth is 1).
  • ReLU hidden neurons instead of sigmoid: $h = (0.5, 0)$ and $p = 0.62$ — neuron 2 is switched off entirely for this input.
  • All weights 0: both hidden neurons output exactly 0.5 and $p = 0.5$. Worse, both neurons get identical gradients forever, so they never become different — which is why weights start random.

Why it matters in ML: A forward pass is just repeated dot products (Lesson 2) followed by a non-linear function. Stacking layers lets the network build complex features out of simple ones.

7.Backpropagation: the chain rule, backwards

In plain wordsBackpropagation works out, for every weight, how much it contributed to the error — starting at the output and passing the blame backwards layer by layer. Then each weight is nudged to reduce the error.

To update every weight we need $\partial L/\partial(\text{weight})$. The loss depends on the weights through a chain: weight → hidden $z$ → hidden $h$ → output $z$ → $p$ → $L$. The chain rule multiplies the local derivatives along this path. Backpropagation organises it efficiently: compute an "error signal" $\delta$ at the output, then pass it backwards layer by layer, reusing each result.

  1. Output error. For sigmoid + log loss, Lesson 8 showed the derivative w.r.t. the output's $z$ simplifies to $\delta_{\text{out}} = p - y$.
  2. Output weights. $\frac{\partial L}{\partial v_j} = \delta_{\text{out}}\cdot h_j$ and $\frac{\partial L}{\partial c} = \delta_{\text{out}}$.
  3. Pass the error back. Each hidden neuron gets the output error times the weight connecting it, times its own activation derivative: $\delta_j = \delta_{\text{out}}\cdot v_j\cdot g'(z_j)$.
  4. Hidden weights. $\frac{\partial L}{\partial W_{jk}} = \delta_j\cdot x_k$ and $\frac{\partial L}{\partial b_j} = \delta_j$.
  5. Update all weights with gradient descent: $w \leftarrow w - \eta\,\frac{\partial L}{\partial w}$.

Every gradient has the same pattern: (error signal arriving at a neuron) × (input that came into it).

Worked example — backward pass and one update

Continuing from the forward pass ($p = 0.5609$, $y = 1$, $h = (0.6225, 0.3775)$).

1. Output error: $\delta_{\text{out}} = 0.5609 - 1 = -0.4391$.

2. Output weights: $\frac{\partial L}{\partial v_1} = -0.4391\times0.6225 \approx -0.2733$, $\ \frac{\partial L}{\partial v_2} = -0.4391\times0.3775 \approx -0.1658$, $\ \frac{\partial L}{\partial c} = -0.4391$.

3. Hidden errors (sigmoid derivative $h(1-h) = 0.6225\times0.3775 \approx 0.2350$ for both):
$\delta_1 = -0.4391\times(1)\times0.2350 \approx -0.1032$
$\delta_2 = -0.4391\times(-1)\times0.2350 \approx +0.1032$

4. Hidden weights: multiply by the inputs $(1, 0)$: neuron 1's gradients are $(-0.1032,\ 0)$, neuron 2's are $(0.1032,\ 0)$. (Weights from $x_2 = 0$ get zero gradient — that input contributed nothing.)

5. Update with $\eta = 1$:
$v = (1 + 0.2733,\ -1 + 0.1658) = (1.2733,\ -0.8342)$, $\ c = 0.4391$
neuron 1: $(0.5 + 0.1032,\ 0.3) = (0.6032,\ 0.3)$; neuron 2: $(-0.5 - 0.1032,\ 0.8) = (-0.6032,\ 0.8)$

Check: running the forward pass again gives $p \approx 0.7245$ and loss $\approx 0.322$ (down from 0.578). One step of backpropagation made the network noticeably more confident in the right answer.

Make sense of it

The situation: The network gave 56% to the right answer. Backpropagation works out how much each weight was to blame, and nudges each one.

What the result tells you: The output error −0.44 says "too low". It flows back through each weight: weights that pushed the wrong way get the biggest corrections. After one step the network gives 72%.

What if…?

  • Learning rate 0.1: $p$ rises only to 0.579 (loss 0.547) — a small, safe step.
  • Learning rate 5: $p$ jumps to 0.98 in one step — great on this one example, but steps this big usually make training on many examples unstable.
  • If the truth were 0: every gradient flips sign; one step ($\eta = 1$) lowers $p$ to 0.34 and the loss from 0.82 to 0.41.

Why it matters in ML: Every deep-learning framework does exactly this, automatically, for millions of weights: forward pass, loss, backward pass (the chain rule, Lesson 3), update (gradient descent, Lesson 7).

Why it's efficient

Backpropagation computes the gradients for all weights in roughly the same time as one forward pass, by reusing the $\delta$ values. That's what makes training networks with millions or billions of weights possible. It was popularised for neural networks by Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams in 1986.

Step-by-step derivationDerive the gradient for one hidden weight
  1. $$\frac{\partial L}{\partial W_{jk}} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial z}\cdot\frac{\partial z}{\partial h_j}\cdot\frac{\partial h_j}{\partial z_j}\cdot\frac{\partial z_j}{\partial W_{jk}}$$

    Chain rule along the path $W_{jk} \to z_j \to h_j \to z \to L$.

  2. $$\frac{\partial L}{\partial z} = p - y$$

    Sigmoid output with log loss (Lesson 8).

  3. $$\frac{\partial z}{\partial h_j} = v_j$$

    Because $z = \sum_j v_jh_j + c$.

  4. $$\frac{\partial h_j}{\partial z_j} = g'(z_j)$$

    The hidden activation's derivative.

  5. $$\frac{\partial z_j}{\partial W_{jk}} = x_k$$

    Because $z_j = \sum_k W_{jk}x_k + b_j$.

  6. $$\frac{\partial L}{\partial W_{jk}} = \underbrace{(p - y)\,v_j\,g'(z_j)}_{\delta_j}\cdot x_k$$

    Multiply: error signal × input — exactly the backprop rule.

Advanced · optionalThe softmax + cross-entropy gradient

With $K$ classes, the output layer computes $p_k = e^{z_k}/\sum_j e^{z_j}$ and the loss for a one-hot label $\mathbf{y}$ is $\ell = -\sum_k y_k\ln p_k$. The softmax derivative is $\partial p_k/\partial z_j = p_k(\mathbb{1}[k=j] - p_j)$. Therefore

$$\frac{\partial \ell}{\partial z_j} = -\sum_k \frac{y_k}{p_k}\,p_k(\mathbb{1}[k=j]-p_j) = -y_j + p_j\sum_k y_k = p_j - y_j.$$

Exactly the same "prediction minus target" error signal as the sigmoid + log loss in this lesson — which is why softmax and cross-entropy are always paired, and why frameworks fuse them into one numerically stable operation.

8.The same thing with matrices

In plain wordsThe same calculations are written with matrices so that the computer can process many examples at once.

For a batch of $n$ examples (rows of $X$), with tanh hidden units and a sigmoid output:

$$H = \tanh(XW_1 + \mathbf{b}_1), \qquad P = \sigma(HW_2 + b_2)$$

Backward:

$$\Delta_2 = \tfrac{1}{n}(P - Y), \quad \frac{\partial L}{\partial W_2} = H^\top\Delta_2, \quad \Delta_1 = (\Delta_2W_2^\top)\odot(1 - H^2), \quad \frac{\partial L}{\partial W_1} = X^\top\Delta_1$$

($\odot$ means element-wise multiplication; $1 - H^2$ is tanh's derivative.) These four lines are exactly what the NumPy code below does.

9.Try it: train a neural network

A small network with one hidden layer of tanh neurons learns to separate two classes. Pick a dataset — XOR, circle or spiral — and a number of hidden neurons, then press Train. The background shows the network's predicted probability. With 1 hidden neuron it can only draw a straight line; add neurons and watch it bend the boundary. The spiral needs the most neurons — and the most training: press Train again if it hasn't finished.

10.Training in practice

  • Initialisation: start weights as small random numbers, never all equal. If every weight is the same, every hidden neuron computes the same thing and gets the same gradient — they'd never become different.
  • Scale inputs (standardise), as with any gradient-descent model.
  • Mini-batches and epochs (Lesson 7): update on small random batches; one epoch is one pass over the data.
  • Watch the validation loss and stop when it starts rising (early stopping); use L2 regularization (Lesson 10).
  • Size: more neurons and layers give more capacity — and more risk of overfitting.
Universal approximation

A famous result says that a network with just one hidden layer and enough neurons can approximate any reasonable continuous function as closely as you like. It doesn't say how many neurons you'd need, or that training will find the right weights — in practice, deeper networks with fewer neurons per layer usually learn much more efficiently.

11.In Python: a network from scratch

A 2-4-1 network learning XOR with NumPy — every line corresponds to an equation above:

import numpy as np

X = np.array([[0, 0], [0, 1], [1, 0], [1, 1]], dtype=float)
Y = np.array([[0], [1], [1], [0]], dtype=float)

def sigmoid(z):
    return 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
W1 = rng.normal(0, 1, (2, 4)); b1 = np.zeros(4)     # input -> 4 hidden neurons
W2 = rng.normal(0, 1, (4, 1)); b2 = np.zeros(1)     # hidden -> output
lr = 0.5

for step in range(5001):
    # forward pass
    H = np.tanh(X @ W1 + b1)
    P = sigmoid(H @ W2 + b2)
    loss = -np.mean(Y * np.log(P) + (1 - Y) * np.log(1 - P))
    # backward pass (backpropagation)
    dZ2 = (P - Y) / len(X)
    dW2 = H.T @ dZ2;  db2 = dZ2.sum(axis=0)
    dZ1 = (dZ2 @ W2.T) * (1 - H ** 2)          # tanh'(z) = 1 - tanh(z)^2
    dW1 = X.T @ dZ1;  db1 = dZ1.sum(axis=0)
    # gradient descent update
    W1 -= lr * dW1;  b1 -= lr * db1
    W2 -= lr * dW2;  b2 -= lr * db2
    if step in (0, 1000, 5000):
        print(step, round(loss, 4))

print(P.round(3).ravel())

Output:

0 0.6712
1000 0.0051
5000 0.0009
[0.    0.999 0.999 0.002]

The loss falls from 0.67 (guessing) to almost 0, and the predictions for $(0,0), (0,1), (1,0), (1,1)$ are essentially $0, 1, 1, 0$ — XOR, solved by a hidden layer.

With scikit-learn, on the 8×8 handwritten digits (64 inputs, 10 classes):

from sklearn.datasets import load_digits
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.neural_network import MLPClassifier
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline

X, y = load_digits(return_X_y=True)
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.25, stratify=y, random_state=0)

mlp = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(),
                    MLPClassifier(hidden_layer_sizes=(64,), max_iter=500, random_state=0))
mlp.fit(X_train, y_train)
print(round(mlp.score(X_train, y_train), 3), round(mlp.score(X_test, y_test), 3))

Output: 1.0 0.973. One hidden layer of 64 ReLU neurons (scikit-learn's default activation) — $64\times64 + 64 + 64\times10 + 10 = 4{,}810$ parameters — reaches 97.3% on unseen digits, a little above logistic regression on the same split (96.9%). The 100% training score hints at mild overfitting; increasing alpha (L2) or using early_stopping=True are the usual remedies.

12.Running example: Chennai Homes

A tiny neural network (one hidden layer of 4 neurons) learns to predict fast sales from size, distance and age, getting every house right even in leave-one-out evaluation. On such small, simple data, though, the decision tree's rule works just as well and is far easier to explain.

Same 12 houses as Lesson 1. With so little data, treat the numbers as an illustration of the method, not as reliable estimates.

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
df = pd.read_csv("houses.csv")   # download it from Lesson 1
from sklearn.neural_network import MLPClassifier
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score, LeaveOneOut
cols = ["size_m2", "dist_km", "age_yrs"]
mlp = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), MLPClassifier(hidden_layer_sizes=(4,), max_iter=5000, random_state=0))
print("training accuracy:", mlp.fit(df[cols], df["sold_fast"]).score(df[cols], df["sold_fast"]))
print("leave-one-out accuracy:", round(cross_val_score(mlp, df[cols], df["sold_fast"], cv=LeaveOneOut()).mean(), 2))

Output:

training accuracy: 1.0
leave-one-out accuracy: 1.0

⇄ Compare side by side: Classical machine learning vs deep learning

Where this is used
  • Handwriting and image recognition
  • The foundation of every modern deep learning system

Choose it when: Large datasets with complex patterns, especially images, audio and text.

Think twice when: Small tabular datasets — gradient boosting or logistic regression are usually better and simpler.

Misconceptions to unlearn

MythNeural networks work like the human brain.

RealityThey're loosely inspired by neurons, but they are mathematical functions trained by gradient descent.

MythDeeper networks are always better.

RealityMore depth needs more data and careful training; on small tabular data, simple models often win.

Responsible AI · Fragile and opaque

Neural networks can be fooled by tiny, deliberately chosen changes to their input: Szegedy et al. (2014) and Goodfellow et al. (2015) showed images altered imperceptibly to humans that networks misclassify with high confidence. Their reasoning is also hard to inspect. For safety-critical uses, test robustness, monitor behaviour after deployment, and don't treat confidence as correctness.

13.Questions beginners often ask

How many layers and neurons should I use?

Start small (one or two hidden layers), check for underfitting or overfitting, and grow or regularise from there.

Why ReLU instead of sigmoid in hidden layers?

ReLU is cheap and its gradient doesn't shrink for positive inputs, so deep networks train much better.

Is a neural network always better?

No. On small tabular datasets, gradient boosting or logistic regression is often more accurate and far simpler.

Common mistakes to avoid
  • Initialising all weights to the same value (usually zero).
  • Forgetting non-linear activations between layers.
  • Not scaling inputs, which slows or stalls training.
Interview corner

Don't confuse

  • Activation function vs loss function — Inside the network vs at the end.
  • Forward pass vs backward pass — Predict, then assign blame.
  • Dropout vs batch normalisation — Random silence vs steady scaling.

Hidden questions — answer in your head first, then open.

Why does a neural network need non-linear activation functions?

The trap: "To make outputs between 0 and 1."

Without them, stacked layers collapse into a single linear layer: $W_2(W_1\mathbf{x}) = (W_2W_1)\mathbf{x}$. However deep, the network could only draw straight boundaries. The non-linearity is what lets depth build complex functions.

What happens if you initialise all weights to zero?

The trap: "Training just starts slowly."

Every neuron in a layer computes the same output and receives the same gradient, so they stay identical forever — the layer behaves like a single neuron. Random initialisation breaks this symmetry. (Biases can start at zero.)

Why did sigmoid hidden layers make deep networks hard to train?

The trap: Blaming the data.

The sigmoid's slope is at most 0.25, and nearly 0 for large inputs. Backpropagation multiplies one such factor per layer, so gradients shrink exponentially in early layers: the vanishing-gradient problem. ReLU (slope 1 for positive inputs), careful initialisation, batch normalisation and residual connections fixed it.

What is a "dying ReLU"?

The trap: Thinking ReLU has no downsides.

If a neuron's input becomes negative for every example (often after a large update), it outputs 0 and gets zero gradient, so it never recovers. Lower learning rates, careful initialisation or Leaky ReLU help.

All 8 hidden questions for this lesson →

14.Key takeaways

  • A neuron computes $g(\mathbf{w}\cdot\mathbf{x} + b)$; layers of neurons are matrix multiplications plus activations.
  • Non-linear activations (ReLU, tanh, sigmoid) are what make hidden layers useful — they let networks solve problems like XOR.
  • Backpropagation is the chain rule: compute $\delta_{\text{out}} = p - y$, pass errors backwards ($\delta_j = \delta_{\text{out}}v_jg'(z_j)$), and each gradient = error × input.
  • Training = forward pass, loss, backward pass, gradient-descent update, repeated over mini-batches.
  • Initialise randomly, scale inputs, and watch validation loss to avoid overfitting.

15.Check your understanding

1. Why can't a single neuron learn XOR?

The 1s and 0s lie on opposite diagonals; separating them needs at least two lines combined, i.e. a hidden layer.

2. What happens if you remove all activation functions from a deep network?

A chain of linear maps is still linear: $V(W\mathbf{x}) = (VW)\mathbf{x}$.

3. What is ReLU(−3)?

$\max(0, -3) = 0$.

4. Output $p = 0.8$, label $y = 0$, hidden activation $h_1 = 0.5$. What is $\partial L/\partial v_1$ (sigmoid + log loss)?

$\delta_{\text{out}} = p - y = 0.8$; $\partial L/\partial v_1 = 0.8\times0.5 = 0.4$. Positive, so $v_1$ will decrease.

5. Why must weights be initialised randomly rather than all zeros?

Random initialisation "breaks the symmetry" so each hidden neuron can specialise.

Answers can be decimals (round to 3 places), fractions like 2/3 or percentages like 75%. Every answer has been checked with Python. Exercise 1By hand

Inputs $\mathbf{x} = (2, 1)$. Hidden ReLU neurons with weights $(1, -1)$ and $(-1, 2)$, biases 0. Output sigmoid with weights $(2, 3)$, bias $-1$. Compute the output.

Check your answer:

Show solution
$h_1 = \text{ReLU}(2 - 1) = 1$; $h_2 = \text{ReLU}(-2 + 2) = 0$. $z = 2\cdot1 + 3\cdot0 - 1 = 1$; $p = \sigma(1) \approx 0.731$.
Exercise 2By hand

Continue exercise 1 with label $y = 0$. Compute $\partial L/\partial v_1$ and $\partial L/\partial v_2$ (sigmoid + log loss).

Check your answers:

Show solution
$\delta_{\text{out}} = p - y = 0.731$. $\partial L/\partial v_1 = 0.731\times h_1 = 0.731$; $\partial L/\partial v_2 = 0.731\times0 = 0$ (neuron 2 was inactive).
Exercise 3By hand

How many parameters has a network with 10 inputs, hidden layers of 32 and 16 neurons, and 3 outputs?

Check your answer:

Show solution
$(10\cdot32 + 32) + (32\cdot16 + 16) + (16\cdot3 + 3) = 352 + 528 + 51 = 931$.
Exercise 4Code

In the XOR code, change the hidden size from 4 to 1 ((2, 1) and (1, 1)) and run it. Can it learn XOR? Why?

Show solution
No — the loss stays high and at least one point is misclassified. One hidden neuron draws one line, and XOR needs two.

Lesson 19: Deep Learning Architectures

Training deep nets, CNNs for images, RNNs for sequences, and Transformers.

By the end of this lesson you can

  • Explain vanishing gradients and the techniques that fix them
  • Compute a convolution, output sizes and max pooling by hand
  • Describe how RNNs and LSTMs process sequences
  • Compute scaled dot-product attention for a small example
Before you start

This lesson builds on:

  • Lesson 10: Overfitting, Regularization & Bias–Variance — Error = bias² + variance + noise. Regularization adds a penalty on weight size (L2 ridge shrinks weights; L1 lasso zeros some) to reduce variance; its strength is chosen by cross-validation.
  • Lesson 18: Neural Networks from Scratch — A neural network stacks layers of neurons $g(W\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{b})$. Backpropagation (the chain rule) gives every weight's gradient, and gradient descent updates them.

Where this fits: How the ideas of Lesson 18 scale up to the deep learning behind modern image recognition and language models.

1.What makes learning "deep"?

Deep learning means neural networks with many layers. Each layer builds on the previous one: in an image network, early layers detect edges, middle layers combine edges into textures and shapes, and later layers recognise eyes, wheels or letters. The network learns this hierarchy of features by itself, from data.

Lesson 18's fully connected network treats every input independently. For images, sound and text that wastes structure we know is there — nearby pixels belong together; word order matters. Deep learning's big successes come from architectures built around that structure: convolutional networks for images, recurrent networks for sequences, and Transformers, which now power language models. This lesson explains how each works, plus the techniques that make deep networks trainable.

2.Making deep networks trainable

In plain wordsDeep networks are hard to train because the learning signal can fade as it travels back through many layers. ReLU activations, careful starting weights, normalisation layers, shortcut connections and smart optimisers like Adam fix this; dropout reduces overfitting.

Vanishing gradients

Backpropagation multiplies derivatives layer by layer (Lesson 18). The sigmoid's derivative is at most $0.25$. Through 10 sigmoid layers, a gradient can shrink by a factor of up to $0.25^{10} \approx 0.000001$ — the early layers barely learn. This vanishing gradient problem held deep learning back for years. Fixes:

  • ReLU activations: derivative exactly 1 for positive inputs, so gradients pass through undiminished.
  • Careful initialisation: scale random initial weights to the layer size (e.g. "He" or "Glorot" initialisation) so signals neither explode nor vanish.
  • Normalisation layers (batch norm, layer norm): rescale each layer's activations to a stable range during training.
  • Residual (skip) connections: compute $\mathbf{h} + f(\mathbf{h})$ instead of $f(\mathbf{h})$, giving gradients a shortcut path. These made networks with 100+ layers possible.

Better optimisers

Momentum keeps a running average of past gradients, so steps build speed in consistent directions and damp oscillations — like a ball rolling downhill. Adam (Kingma & Ba, ICLR 2015) combines momentum with a per-parameter step size, adapted from running averages of the gradient $g$ and the squared gradient:

$$m \leftarrow \beta_1 m + (1-\beta_1)g, \qquad s \leftarrow \beta_2 s + (1-\beta_2)g^2, \qquad w \leftarrow w - \eta\,\frac{\hat{m}}{\sqrt{\hat{s}} + \epsilon}$$

($\hat{m}, \hat{s}$ are bias-corrected versions of $m, s$; typical values are $\beta_1 = 0.9$, $\beta_2 = 0.999$.) Parameters with consistently large gradients take smaller steps, and rarely-updated ones take larger steps. Adam is the default optimiser in most deep learning work.

Fighting overfitting

  • Dropout: during training, randomly switch off a fraction of neurons (e.g. 20–50%) at each step. No neuron can rely on any specific other neuron, which acts like training an ensemble of many thinner networks (Lesson 14).
  • Data augmentation: create extra training examples by flipping, cropping or slightly rotating images — the label stays the same.
  • Early stopping and weight decay (L2), as before.

3.Convolutional neural networks (CNNs)

A 224×224 colour image has $224\times224\times3 = 150{,}528$ inputs. A fully connected layer of just 1,000 neurons would need 150 million weights — and it would have to learn "cat ear" separately for every position in the image. CNNs fix this with two ideas:

  • Local connections: each neuron looks only at a small patch (e.g. 3×3 pixels).
  • Weight sharing: the same small set of weights — a filter or kernel — is slid across the whole image. A feature detector learned in one place works everywhere.

The convolution operation

Slide the kernel over the image. At each position, multiply the overlapping numbers element by element and add them up; that sum is one pixel of the output, called a feature map.

$$\text{out}[i, j] = \sum_{u}\sum_{v}\text{image}[i + u,\ j + v]\cdot\text{kernel}[u, v]$$
Worked example — detecting a vertical edge

A 4×6 image: dark (0) on the left, bright (9) on the right. A 3×3 vertical-edge kernel:

$$\text{image} = \begin{bmatrix}0&0&0&9&9&9\\0&0&0&9&9&9\\0&0&0&9&9&9\\0&0&0&9&9&9\end{bmatrix} \qquad \text{kernel} = \begin{bmatrix}-1&0&1\\-1&0&1\\-1&0&1\end{bmatrix}$$

The kernel computes (right column − left column) of each 3×3 window.

  • Window over columns 1–3 (all 0s): $0$.
  • Window over columns 2–4: left column 0s, right column 9s: $3\times9 - 0 = 27$.
  • Window over columns 3–5: left 0s, right 9s again: $27$.
  • Window over columns 4–6 (all 9s): $3\times9 - 3\times9 = 0$.
$$\text{feature map} = \begin{bmatrix}0 & 27 & 27 & 0\\ 0 & 27 & 27 & 0\end{bmatrix}$$

The output "lights up" exactly where the edge is and is 0 in flat regions. A CNN learns its kernel values by backpropagation, discovering whatever detectors are useful.

Make sense of it

The situation: A phone camera app needs to find the edge of a document in a photo. A 3×3 kernel slides across the image looking for a jump from dark to bright.

What the result tells you: The feature map is 27 where the window straddles the edge and 0 in flat areas. Big value = "edge here".

What if…?

  • Bright on the left, dark on the right: the map becomes −27. The sign tells you the direction of the edge.
  • A faint edge (0 to 1 instead of 0 to 9): the response is only 3. The size tells you the strength.
  • A horizontal edge (dark top, bright bottom): this vertical-edge kernel gives 0 everywhere. You need a different kernel — so CNNs learn many.

Why it matters in ML: The same small kernel is reused at every position, so a CNN needs few weights and finds a pattern wherever it appears. Early layers learn edges like this; later layers combine them into shapes and objects.

Output size, stride and padding

For input width $W$, kernel size $F$, padding $P$ (zeros added around the border) and stride $S$ (step size):

$$W_{\text{out}} = \frac{W - F + 2P}{S} + 1$$

Example above: $(6 - 3 + 0)/1 + 1 = 4$ ✓. With a 28×28 image, $F = 3$, $P = 1$, $S = 1$: $(28 - 3 + 2)/1 + 1 = 28$ — "same" padding keeps the size.

Channels and parameter counts

A colour image has 3 channels (red, green, blue), so a 3×3 kernel actually has $3\times3\times3 = 27$ weights plus a bias. A layer usually has many kernels, each producing its own feature map. 16 kernels: $(27 + 1)\times16 = 448$ parameters. Compare a fully connected layer from a 32×32×3 image to just 16 neurons: $3072\times16 + 16 = 49{,}168$. Weight sharing makes CNNs over 100 times leaner here.

Pooling

Max pooling shrinks a feature map by keeping only the largest value in each small window, usually 2×2 with stride 2. It keeps "was the feature present around here?" while discarding the exact position, and cuts the size by 4×, which discards 75% of the activations.

Worked example — 2×2 max pooling
$$\begin{bmatrix}1&3&2&0\\4&6&1&1\\0&2&5&7\\1&1&3&2\end{bmatrix} \xrightarrow{\ \text{max pool}\ } \begin{bmatrix}6 & 2\\ 2 & 7\end{bmatrix}$$

Top-left window $\{1, 3, 4, 6\}$ → 6; top-right $\{2, 0, 1, 1\}$ → 2; bottom-left $\{0, 2, 1, 1\}$ → 2; bottom-right $\{5, 7, 3, 2\}$ → 7.

Make sense of it

The situation: After finding edges, the network only needs to know roughly where each one is, not to the exact pixel.

What the result tells you: Each 2×2 window keeps only its strongest response, so the map shrinks to a quarter of its size while keeping the important signals.

What if…?

  • Move the 6 one pixel within its window: the output is still 6. Small shifts don't change the result.
  • Average pooling instead: 3.5, 1, 1, 4.25 — smoother, but weak signals dilute strong ones.

Why it matters in ML: Pooling makes CNNs cheaper and more tolerant of small shifts in position. Many modern networks use strided convolutions instead, but the idea is the same.

A typical CNN

[conv → ReLU → pool] repeated several times (feature maps get smaller but more numerous), then flatten, then one or two fully connected layers, then softmax over the classes.

Step-by-step derivationWhere the output-size formula comes from
  1. $$W + 2P$$

    Padding adds $P$ zeros on each side, so the padded width is $W + 2P$.

  2. $$0,\ S,\ 2S,\ \dots,\ (W + 2P - F)$$

    The kernel's left edge can start at these positions: it must still fit, so the last start is $W + 2P - F$.

  3. $$\frac{W + 2P - F}{S} + 1$$

    Count the positions: the number of steps of size $S$, plus 1 for the starting position.

4.Try it: convolution explorer

Left: a real 8×8 handwritten digit from scikit-learn's digits dataset. Choose a kernel and see the feature map it produces (right). Green = strong positive response, red = strong negative. The vertical-edge kernel lights up the left and right edges of the strokes; the horizontal one finds tops and bottoms. Hover over the output to see the exact sum for that position.

5.Recurrent neural networks (RNNs)

Text, speech, sensor readings and prices are sequences: order matters, and lengths vary. An RNN reads a sequence one step at a time, carrying a hidden state $\mathbf{h}_t$ — a memory of what it has seen so far:

$$\mathbf{h}_t = \tanh\big(W_h\mathbf{h}_{t-1} + W_x\mathbf{x}_t + \mathbf{b}\big)$$

The same weights are used at every step (weight sharing again, this time across time). The final state, or the state at each step, feeds an output layer — e.g. to classify a review as positive or negative, or to predict the next word.

The problem: training backpropagates through every time step, multiplying by $W_h$ again and again, so gradients vanish (or explode) over long sequences. Plain RNNs struggle to remember things from more than about 10–20 steps back.

LSTMs

The long short-term memory network (Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, 1997) adds a separate cell state — a kind of conveyor belt that information can travel along unchanged — controlled by three gates. Each gate is a sigmoid layer outputting numbers between 0 and 1, multiplied element-wise with the information it controls:

  • the forget gate decides what to erase from the cell state;
  • the input gate decides what new information to write;
  • the output gate decides what part of the cell state to output as $\mathbf{h}_t$.

Because the cell state is updated by addition rather than repeated multiplication, gradients survive over much longer sequences. LSTMs (and the simpler GRUs) dominated sequence tasks until Transformers arrived.

6.Transformers and attention

Picture itAt a busy party you hear your name across the room and instantly tune in to that conversation. Attention lets each word in a sentence tune in to the other words that matter for it, and mostly ignore the rest.

In plain wordsTransformers let every word look at every other word and decide which ones matter for its meaning ("attention"). This works very well and runs fast on GPUs, which is why it powers modern language models.

RNNs process words one at a time, which is slow and makes long-range connections hard. The Transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017, "Attention Is All You Need") is "based solely on attention mechanisms, dispensing with recurrence and convolutions entirely". Every position looks at every other position directly, in one step.

Self-attention

Each word (token) is represented by a vector. From it, the model computes three vectors with learned weight matrices:

  • a query $\mathbf{q}$ — "what am I looking for?",
  • a key $\mathbf{k}$ — "what do I contain?",
  • a value $\mathbf{v}$ — "what do I pass on if selected?".

Each token compares its query with every token's key (dot products — Lesson 2 — measure similarity), turns the scores into weights with softmax (Lesson 8), and takes the weighted average of the values:

$$\text{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \text{softmax}\!\left(\frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V$$

Dividing by $\sqrt{d_k}$ (the key length) keeps the scores from growing too large as vectors get longer.

Worked example — attention over three tokens

Three tokens with 2-dimensional vectors. For simplicity, queries = keys: $\mathbf{q}_1 = \mathbf{k}_1 = (1, 0)$, $\mathbf{q}_2 = \mathbf{k}_2 = (0, 1)$, $\mathbf{q}_3 = \mathbf{k}_3 = (1, 1)$. Values: $\mathbf{v}_1 = (1, 0)$, $\mathbf{v}_2 = (0, 1)$, $\mathbf{v}_3 = (0.5, 0.5)$. Here $d_k = 2$, so we divide by $\sqrt2 \approx 1.414$.

Token 1's scores against keys 1, 2, 3: $\frac{(1,0)\cdot(1,0)}{\sqrt2} = 0.707$, $\ \frac{(1,0)\cdot(0,1)}{\sqrt2} = 0$, $\ \frac{(1,0)\cdot(1,1)}{\sqrt2} = 0.707$.

Softmax: $e^{0.707} \approx 2.03$, $e^0 = 1$, $e^{0.707} \approx 2.03$; total $5.06$. Weights $\approx (0.401,\ 0.198,\ 0.401)$.

Output: $0.401\,(1, 0) + 0.198\,(0, 1) + 0.401\,(0.5, 0.5) \approx (0.602,\ 0.398)$.

Token 1 "attended" most to itself and to token 3, whose keys resemble its query, and its new representation mixes in their values. In a sentence like "The animal didn't cross the street because it was tired", attention lets "it" pull information from "animal".

Make sense of it

The situation: In "The animal didn't cross the street because it was tired", the word "it" must find which earlier word it refers to. Attention lets each word ask the others "are you relevant to me?"

What the result tells you: Token 1's query matches keys 1 and 3 equally, so it takes 40% from each and 20% from token 2. Its new vector (0.60, 0.40) is a blend weighted by relevance.

What if…?

  • Without dividing by $\sqrt{d_k}$: weights (0.42, 0.16, 0.42) — sharper. With 512-dimensional vectors, unscaled scores get huge and softmax becomes almost all-or-nothing, which makes training unstable; that's why the scaling is there.
  • A stronger query (10, 0): weights (0.5, 0.0, 0.5) — it ignores token 2 completely.
  • Token 3's query (1, 1) matches itself most: weights (0.25, 0.25, 0.50).

Why it matters in ML: Attention is dot products (similarity), softmax (turn scores into weights) and a weighted average. That's the core of every Transformer, including large language models.

A Transformer stacks many such layers, each with several attention "heads" running in parallel, plus small feed-forward networks, residual connections and layer normalisation. Since attention itself ignores order, a positional encoding is added to each token's vector. Because all positions are processed at once, Transformers train efficiently on GPUs — which is what made today's large language models possible.

Where things stand now

Large language models, reasoning models, agents and diffusion image generators are all built from the ideas in this lesson. For a dated overview of recent developments — and how each connects back to this course — see Recent developments in LLMs and generative AI.

Advanced · optionalWhy attention divides by √dₖ

Suppose the entries of a query $\mathbf{q}$ and key $\mathbf{k}$ are independent with mean 0 and variance 1. Then $\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{k} = \sum_{i=1}^{d_k} q_ik_i$ is a sum of $d_k$ terms each with mean 0 and variance 1, so

$$\operatorname{Var}(\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{k}) = d_k, \qquad \operatorname{Var}\!\left(\frac{\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{k}}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right) = 1.$$

Without the scaling, with $d_k = 64$ the scores would have standard deviation 8; softmax of such spread-out numbers puts almost all the weight on one token, and its gradients become tiny (the softmax saturates). Dividing by $\sqrt{d_k}$ keeps the scores in a range where attention can spread out and still learn — the reason given in the original Transformer paper (Vaswani et al., 2017).

Read the formulaScaled dot-product attention
$$\text{Attention} = \htmlClass{fd-1}{\text{softmax}}\Big(\frac{\htmlClass{fd-2}{QK^\top}}{\htmlClass{fd-3}{\sqrt{d_k}}}\Big)\htmlClass{fd-4}{V}$$
  • softmax — turns scores into weights that sum to 1
  • QKᵀ — similarity of every query with every key (dot products)
  • √dₖ — keeps scores from growing too large
  • V — the values that get averaged using those weights

Hover over (or tap) a part to highlight it in the formula.

7.Transfer learning: standing on giants' shoulders

Training a large network from scratch needs huge datasets and computing power. Instead, you can take a pretrained model — trained on millions of images or billions of words — and fine-tune it on your smaller dataset. Its early layers already detect general features (edges, word meanings), so you only need to adapt the later layers. This is how most practical deep learning is done today.

8.Tools

scikit-learn's MLPClassifier is fine for small fully connected networks (Lesson 18), but it has no convolutions, recurrence, attention or GPU support. For deep learning, practitioners use PyTorch or TensorFlow/Keras, which compute gradients automatically ("autograd") and run on GPUs.

9.In Python

Convolution, pooling and attention from scratch with NumPy — the same calculations as the worked examples:

import numpy as np

def conv2d(image, kernel):
    kh, kw = kernel.shape
    out = np.zeros((image.shape[0] - kh + 1, image.shape[1] - kw + 1))
    for i in range(out.shape[0]):
        for j in range(out.shape[1]):
            out[i, j] = np.sum(image[i:i+kh, j:j+kw] * kernel)
    return out

image = np.array([[0, 0, 0, 9, 9, 9]] * 4, dtype=float)
edge = np.array([[-1, 0, 1]] * 3, dtype=float)
print(conv2d(image, edge))

fmap = np.array([[1, 3, 2, 0], [4, 6, 1, 1], [0, 2, 5, 7], [1, 1, 3, 2]], dtype=float)
print(fmap.reshape(2, 2, 2, 2).max(axis=(1, 3)))      # 2x2 max pooling

def attention(Q, K, V):
    scores = Q @ K.T / np.sqrt(K.shape[1])
    weights = np.exp(scores) / np.exp(scores).sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)   # softmax per row
    return weights, weights @ V

Q = K = np.array([[1, 0], [0, 1], [1, 1]], dtype=float)
V = np.array([[1, 0], [0, 1], [0.5, 0.5]])
weights, out = attention(Q, K, V)
print(weights.round(3))
print(out.round(3))

Output:

[[ 0. 27. 27.  0.]
 [ 0. 27. 27.  0.]]
[[6. 2.]
 [2. 7.]]
[[0.401 0.198 0.401]
 [0.198 0.401 0.401]
 [0.248 0.248 0.503]]
[[0.602 0.398]
 [0.398 0.602]
 [0.5   0.5  ]]

Every number matches the worked examples. For reference, this is what a small CNN for 28×28 grayscale digits looks like in PyTorch. This snippet was not run as part of this course's checks — PyTorch must be installed separately (see pytorch.org).

import torch.nn as nn

model = nn.Sequential(
    nn.Conv2d(1, 16, kernel_size=3, padding=1),   # 28x28x1  -> 28x28x16
    nn.ReLU(),
    nn.MaxPool2d(2),                              # -> 14x14x16
    nn.Conv2d(16, 32, kernel_size=3, padding=1),  # -> 14x14x32
    nn.ReLU(),
    nn.MaxPool2d(2),                              # -> 7x7x32
    nn.Flatten(),                                 # -> 1568 numbers
    nn.Dropout(0.25),
    nn.Linear(32 * 7 * 7, 10),                    # one score per digit
)

10.Running example: Chennai Homes

Deep learning would use the richer data we've ignored: a CNN could learn from photos of each house, and a Transformer could read the listings. Here's what a Transformer would see — a sequence of tokens; with 12 short listings the vocabulary is only 23 words, far too little to train one from scratch, so in practice you'd fine-tune a pretrained language model.

Same 12 houses as Lesson 1. With so little data, treat the numbers as an illustration of the method, not as reliable estimates.

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
df = pd.read_csv("houses.csv")   # download it from Lesson 1
# A Transformer would read the listing text word by word; here we just look at what it would see.
for d in df["description"].head(3):
    tokens = d.split()
    print(len(tokens), "tokens:", tokens)
print("vocabulary size:", len({w for d in df["description"] for w in d.split()}))

Output:

⇄ Compare side by side: Classical machine learning vs deep learning

Where this is used
  • Image recognition (CNNs)
  • Speech recognition and translation
  • Chatbots and large language models (Transformers)

Choose it when: Images, audio, video and text — especially starting from a pretrained model.

Think twice when: Small structured datasets, or when you need a cheap, explainable model.

Misconceptions to unlearn

MythDeep learning always needs millions of examples.

RealityFine-tuning a pretrained model can work with a few hundred or thousand labelled examples.

MythAttention shows exactly why a model made its decision.

RealityAttention weights are one internal signal, not a complete explanation of the model's reasoning.

Responsible AI · Generative models raise new questions

Models that generate text and images inherit the biases of their training data, can produce fluent but false statements ("hallucinations"), and make convincing fake media easy to create. Their training data raises questions of consent and copyright that courts and regulators are still working through. See Recent developments for a dated overview.

11.Questions beginners often ask

Do I need a GPU?

For training large networks on images or text, yes in practice. For small experiments and for fine-tuning small pretrained models, a CPU can be enough.

What's the difference between a CNN and a Transformer?

CNNs look at local patches with shared filters — ideal for images. Transformers let every position attend to every other — ideal for sequences like text, and now also used for images.

Should I train from scratch?

Rarely. Fine-tuning a pretrained model needs far less data and computing power.

Common mistakes to avoid
  • Training a large network from scratch when a pretrained model could be fine-tuned.
  • Forgetting to switch dropout off when evaluating (in PyTorch: model.eval()).
  • Using sigmoid in every layer of a deep network (vanishing gradients) — prefer ReLU in hidden layers.
Interview corner

Don't confuse

  • CNN vs RNN vs Transformer — Grids, chains, all-to-all.
  • Fine-tuning vs feature extraction — Use it as-is vs adjust it.
  • Padding vs stride — Padding adds space; stride skips.

Hidden questions — answer in your head first, then open.

Why do CNNs need far fewer parameters than dense networks on images?

The trap: "Convolutions are just efficient."

Weight sharing: one small kernel is reused at every position. A 3×3 convolution from 3 to 64 channels has 1,792 parameters whatever the image size; a dense layer from a 224×224×3 image to just 64 units needs 9,633,856.

Why does attention divide by $\sqrt{d_k}$?

The trap: "For normalisation", with no explanation.

Dot products of random $d_k$-dimensional vectors have a spread that grows like $\sqrt{d_k}$. Without scaling, large scores push softmax towards all-or-nothing, where its gradients vanish. Dividing keeps scores in a range where softmax is still sensitive.

Why do Transformers need positional encodings?

The trap: Assuming attention knows word order.

Attention treats its inputs as a set: shuffle the tokens and each output is just shuffled too. "Dog bites man" and "man bites dog" would look the same. Positional encodings (fixed or learned) add order information.

Why did LSTMs replace simple RNNs, and why did Transformers largely replace LSTMs?

The trap: Naming them without the reasons.

Simple RNNs suffer vanishing gradients over long sequences; LSTMs' gates and cell state carry information further. Transformers then removed the step-by-step recurrence: attention connects any two positions directly and trains in parallel on GPUs.

All 7 hidden questions for this lesson →

12.Key takeaways

  • Deep networks learn a hierarchy of features. ReLU, good initialisation, normalisation and residual connections fight vanishing gradients; Adam and dropout help training and generalization.
  • CNNs slide small shared kernels over images: output size $(W - F + 2P)/S + 1$; pooling downsamples.
  • RNNs carry a hidden state through a sequence; LSTMs use gates and a cell state to remember longer.
  • Transformers use self-attention, $\text{softmax}(QK^\top/\sqrt{d_k})V$, so every token can look at every other token at once.
  • In practice, start from a pretrained model and fine-tune it.

13.Check your understanding

1. A 32×32 input, 5×5 kernel, padding 0, stride 1. What is the output width?

$(32 - 5 + 0)/1 + 1 = 28$.

2. Why do CNNs need far fewer parameters than fully connected networks on images?

Weight sharing: one 3×3 kernel's few weights are reused at every location.

3. What problem do LSTMs solve compared with plain RNNs?

The gated cell state lets information and gradients flow across many time steps.

4. In self-attention, how is the similarity between a query and a key measured?

Scores are $\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{k}/\sqrt{d_k}$, then softmax turns them into weights.

5. 2×2 max pooling on $\begin{bmatrix}1&5\\3&2\end{bmatrix}$ gives…

Max pooling keeps the largest value in the window: 5.

Show solution

Exercise 2By hand

Convolve $\begin{bmatrix}1&2&0\\0&1&3\\2&1&0\end{bmatrix}$ with the 2×2 kernel $\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{bmatrix}$ (no padding, stride 1).

Check your answer — for several numbers, separate them with commas:

Show solution
Each output = top-left − bottom-right of the window: $1 - 1 = 0$, $2 - 3 = -1$, $0 - 1 = -1$, $1 - 0 = 1$. Result $\begin{bmatrix}0 & -1\\-1 & 1\end{bmatrix}$.

Part 5 · Neural networks & real projects · ~70 min

Lesson 20: Feature Engineering, Pipelines & Final Project

Clean and encode data, build leak-proof pipelines, and complete an end-to-end project.

By the end of this lesson you can

  • Scale, transform and encode features correctly
  • Handle missing values without leaking information
  • Build leak-proof pipelines with ColumnTransformer
  • Complete an end-to-end ML project from raw data to a saved model
Before you start

This lesson builds on:

  • Lesson 5: Data, Features & Generalization — Always judge a model on data it hasn't seen: split into train / validation / test, or use k-fold cross-validation. Overfitting = low training error but high test error. Never let test data leak into training.
  • Lesson 9: Evaluating Models — Accuracy can mislead. Precision $= TP/(TP+FP)$, recall $= TP/(TP+FN)$, and F1 balances them. Moving the threshold trades one for the other; ROC-AUC summarises all thresholds.
  • Lesson 10: Overfitting, Regularization & Bias–Variance — Error = bias² + variance + noise. Regularization adds a penalty on weight size (L2 ridge shrinks weights; L1 lasso zeros some) to reduce variance; its strength is chosen by cross-validation.

Where this fits: Brings everything together into a real project: preparing messy data, building leak-proof pipelines, choosing and evaluating a model, and deploying it.

1.Data beats algorithms

Every model in this course expects a neat table of numbers: no gaps, no text, sensible scales. Real data is never like that. It has missing values, categories like "Chennai" or "two-year contract", amounts that range from 5 to 5 million, and dates. Turning raw data into good model inputs is called feature engineering, and in practice it often matters more than which algorithm you choose.

This final lesson covers the essential techniques, then shows how to package every step into a pipeline that is safe from data leakage. It ends with a complete project — from raw data to a saved, tested model — that puts the whole course together.

2.Numeric features

Scaling

From Lessons 7, 10, 11 and 15: distance-based and gradient-based models (kNN, SVMs, linear and logistic regression, neural networks) need features on similar scales. Tree models (Lessons 13–14) don't.

  • Standardisation (StandardScaler): $z = (x - \mu)/\sigma$ — mean 0, standard deviation 1. The usual default.
  • Min–max scaling (MinMaxScaler): $x' = (x - x_{\min})/(x_{\max} - x_{\min})$ — squeezes into $[0, 1]$.
  • Robust scaling (RobustScaler): uses the median and interquartile range, so outliers don't distort it.
Worked example — standardising tenure

Three customers have been with the company 3, 12 and 24 months. Mean $\mu = 13$. Standard deviation $\sigma = \sqrt{\frac{(-10)^2 + 1^2 + 11^2}{3}} = \sqrt{74} \approx 8.60$.

z-scores: $\frac{3-13}{8.60} \approx -1.16$, $\ \frac{12-13}{8.60} \approx -0.12$, $\ \frac{24-13}{8.60} \approx 1.28$.

Crucially, $\mu$ and $\sigma$ are computed on the training set only, then reused unchanged on the test set and on new data.

Make sense of it

The situation: A telecom company's churn model uses tenure (months with the company). It must be put on a standard scale before training.

What the result tells you: The z-scores say how many standard deviations each customer is from the average: −1.16 is short tenure, +1.28 is long.

What if…?

  • A new customer with 60 months: $z = (60 - 13)/8.60 = 5.46$ — far outside anything seen in training. Worth flagging: the model is extrapolating.
  • One long-standing customer (120 months) in the training data: the mean becomes 39.75 and the standard deviation 46.9, so the original three get z-scores −0.78, −0.59 and −0.34. One outlier squashes everyone else together — robust scaling (median and IQR) avoids this.

Why it matters in ML: Compute the mean and standard deviation on the training data only and reuse them — otherwise information from the test set leaks into training and your scores are over-optimistic.

Transforming skewed values

Amounts like income, prices or total spending are often skewed: most values are small, a few are huge. A log transform compresses the range so the huge values don't dominate: 100, 1,000 and 10,000 become 2, 3 and 4 with $\log_{10}$. In code, np.log1p(x) computes $\ln(1 + x)$, which also handles zeros safely.

Binning

Sometimes it helps to turn a number into ranges (age 18–25, 26–40, …) — useful when the effect isn't smooth, or for readability. It throws away detail, so use it deliberately.

Read the formulaStandardising with training statistics
$$z = \frac{\htmlClass{fd-1}{x} - \htmlClass{fd-2}{\mu_{\text{train}}}}{\htmlClass{fd-3}{\sigma_{\text{train}}}}$$
  • x — any value — training, test or a new customer
  • μ_train — mean learned from the training set only
  • σ_train — standard deviation learned from the training set only

Hover over (or tap) a part to highlight it in the formula.

3.Categorical features

Picture itGiving cities numbers like house numbers on a street would imply Delhi lives "between" Chennai and Mumbai. One-hot encoding gives each city its own light switch instead: on or off.

Models need numbers, but you can't just number the categories (Chennai = 1, Mumbai = 2, Delhi = 3): the model would think Delhi is "three times" Chennai, and that Mumbai lies "between" them.

One-hot encoding

Create one 0/1 column per category; exactly one is 1 for each row.

Worked example
city→city_Chennaicity_Delhicity_Mumbai
Chennai100
Mumbai001
Delhi010

All categories are now equally different from each other. In scikit-learn: OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore") — the option means a category never seen in training (say "Kolkata") becomes all zeros instead of an error.

Make sense of it

The situation: City is a category, not a number. Coding Chennai = 1, Delhi = 2, Mumbai = 3 would tell a linear model that Mumbai is "three times" Chennai.

What the result tells you: One-hot encoding gives each city its own 0/1 column, so no city is "bigger" or "between" others.

What if…?

  • A new city (Kolkata) appears after deployment: with handle_unknown="ignore" it becomes all zeros — the model treats it as "none of the known cities".
  • 1,000 different cities: 1,000 new columns, most almost always 0. Group rare categories into "other", or use target or frequency encoding.

Why it matters in ML: Tree models can cope with simple integer codes; linear models, kNN and neural networks need one-hot (or learned embeddings, Lesson 19).

Ordinal encoding

When categories have a natural order (small < medium < large; month-to-month < one-year < two-year), mapping them to 0, 1, 2 keeps that order in one column (OrdinalEncoder). Fine for trees; for linear models it assumes equal steps between levels.

Many categories

A feature like "postcode" may have thousands of values, which would create thousands of columns. Options include grouping rare categories into "other", or target encoding (replacing each category by the average label for that category — computed carefully inside cross-validation, or it leaks).

4.Missing values

Most scikit-learn models refuse missing values (HistGradientBoosting is an exception). Choices:

  • Drop rows — only if very few are missing and missingness is random. Otherwise you lose data and may bias the sample.
  • Impute — fill in a value with SimpleImputer: the median (robust for numbers), mean, most frequent (for categories), or a constant like "unknown". KNNImputer fills values from similar rows.
  • Add a "was missing" indicator (add_indicator=True). Missingness itself can carry information: a customer who didn't give a phone number may behave differently.
Imputation can leak too

The median used for filling gaps must be computed from the training data only — just like scaling statistics. Pipelines handle this automatically.

5.Creating new features

Often the most valuable features are ones you build from domain knowledge:

  • Ratios and differences: price per m², debt-to-income, monthly charge per support call.
  • Dates: from a timestamp, extract day of week, month, hour, "is weekend", or "days since last purchase". Raw timestamps are rarely useful directly.
  • Interactions: products of features (e.g. PolynomialFeatures) let linear models capture combined effects.
  • Aggregates: a customer's average order value, number of orders in the last 30 days.
  • Text: word counts (CountVectorizer, Lesson 12) or TF-IDF weights, which down-weight words common to every document.
Think like the model

Ask: "If I were predicting this by hand, what would I want to know?" A model predicting late payments benefits from "days until due date" far more than from two separate raw dates.

6.Feature selection

More features isn't always better (Lessons 10, 11, 17). Ways to keep only useful ones: remove near-constant features (VarianceThreshold), keep the best by a statistical test (SelectKBest), keep features a model rates as important (SelectFromModel, e.g. with Lasso), or let L1 regularization zero out the rest. Like all preprocessing, do it inside the pipeline.

7.Try it: a preprocessing pipeline, step by step

Edit the raw customer table (left) — try deleting a monthly charge or changing a city. On the right is the matrix the model actually receives: missing charge filled with the training median, numbers standardised, and the contract one-hot encoded. The statistics shown are "learned" from these rows, exactly what fit does on a training set.

8.Pipelines: preprocessing done right

A Pipeline chains steps into a single model object. A ColumnTransformer applies different steps to different columns. Together they give you three huge benefits:

  1. No leakage. Calling fit learns imputation values, scaling statistics and encodings from the training data only. During cross-validation, they're re-learned inside every fold.
  2. One object to tune. Grid search can tune preprocessing and model settings together (e.g. model__C).
  3. One object to deploy. Raw data in, prediction out — exactly the same transformations in training and production. Mismatches between the two ("training/serving skew") are a classic source of silent bugs.

9.Final project: predicting customer churn

The problem: a telecom company wants to know which customers are likely to cancel ("churn") so it can offer them a deal first. The table has numbers, categories and missing values — like real data. So that you can run everything yourself without downloading anything, the code first generates a realistic dataset of 2,000 customers. (It's synthetic: the patterns were built in, so they illustrate the workflow rather than real customer behaviour.)

Step 1 — Load and explore the data

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
n = 2000
df = pd.DataFrame({
    "tenure_months": rng.integers(1, 73, n),
    "monthly_charge": rng.normal(65, 20, n).clip(15, 130).round(2),
    "support_calls": rng.poisson(1.5, n),
    "contract": rng.choice(["month-to-month", "one-year", "two-year"], n, p=[0.55, 0.25, 0.20]),
    "payment": rng.choice(["card", "bank", "check"], n, p=[0.4, 0.35, 0.25]),
    "city": rng.choice(["Chennai", "Mumbai", "Delhi", "Pune"], n),
})
df["total_spent"] = (df["tenure_months"] * df["monthly_charge"] * rng.normal(1, 0.05, n)).round(2)
score = (-2.0 + 1.6 * (df["contract"] == "month-to-month") - 0.035 * df["tenure_months"]
         + 0.018 * df["monthly_charge"] + 0.45 * df["support_calls"] + 0.5 * (df["payment"] == "check"))
df["churned"] = (rng.random(n) < 1 / (1 + np.exp(-score))).astype(int)
for col, frac in [("monthly_charge", 0.05), ("payment", 0.04)]:     # real data has gaps
    df.loc[rng.random(n) < frac, col] = np.nan

print(df.shape)
print(df.head(3).to_string())
print("churn rate:", round(df["churned"].mean(), 3))
print(df.isna().sum()[df.isna().sum() > 0].to_dict())
(2000, 8)
   tenure_months  monthly_charge  support_calls        contract payment     city  total_spent  churned
0              7           50.16              2        one-year    bank     Pune       316.79        0
1             56           83.49              0  month-to-month     NaN    Delhi      4578.37        1
2             48           65.69              2  month-to-month    card  Chennai      3111.67        1
churn rate: 0.403
{'monthly_charge': 105, 'payment': 86}

2,000 customers, 7 features plus the label. 40% churned, so the classes are only mildly imbalanced. Two columns have gaps (105 and 86 missing values), and three columns are text categories.

Step 2 — Split before anything else

from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

X = df.drop(columns="churned")
y = df["churned"]
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.2, stratify=y, random_state=0)

The test set (400 customers) is now locked away until Step 6 (Lesson 5).

Step 3 — Feature engineering and preprocessing

from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler, OneHotEncoder, FunctionTransformer

def add_features(X):
    X = X.copy()
    X["charge_per_call"] = X["monthly_charge"] / (X["support_calls"] + 1)   # a ratio feature
    X["log_total_spent"] = np.log1p(X["total_spent"])                       # tame the skew
    return X

numeric = ["tenure_months", "monthly_charge", "support_calls", "total_spent",
           "charge_per_call", "log_total_spent"]
categorical = ["contract", "payment", "city"]

preprocess = ColumnTransformer([
    ("num", Pipeline([("impute", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")),
                      ("scale", StandardScaler())]), numeric),
    ("cat", Pipeline([("impute", SimpleImputer(strategy="most_frequent")),
                      ("onehot", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore"))]), categorical),
])

Numbers: fill gaps with the median, then standardise. Categories: fill gaps with the most common value, then one-hot encode. Nothing is fitted yet — that happens inside cross-validation.

Step 4 — Start with a baseline, then compare models

from sklearn.dummy import DummyClassifier
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier, HistGradientBoostingClassifier
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score

candidates = {
    "baseline (majority)": DummyClassifier(strategy="most_frequent"),
    "logistic regression": LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000),
    "random forest": RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=300, random_state=0),
    "gradient boosting": HistGradientBoostingClassifier(random_state=0),
}
for name, clf in candidates.items():
    pipe = Pipeline([("features", FunctionTransformer(add_features)),
                     ("prep", preprocess), ("model", clf)])
    s = cross_val_score(pipe, X_train, y_train, cv=5, scoring="roc_auc")
    print(f"{name:22s} ROC-AUC {s.mean():.3f} ± {s.std():.3f}")
baseline (majority)    ROC-AUC 0.500 ± 0.000
logistic regression    ROC-AUC 0.771 ± 0.008
random forest          ROC-AUC 0.756 ± 0.010
gradient boosting      ROC-AUC 0.739 ± 0.008

We use ROC-AUC (Lesson 9) because we'll want to rank customers by risk. The baseline scores 0.5 — pure guessing — so everything above it is real signal. Interesting: logistic regression beats the ensembles here. The relationships in this data are close to linear on the log-odds scale (Lesson 8), so the simpler model fits them best and the flexible models only add variance. Always compare — don't assume the fanciest model wins.

Step 5 — Tune the best model

from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV

pipe = Pipeline([("features", FunctionTransformer(add_features)), ("prep", preprocess),
                 ("model", LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000))])
search = GridSearchCV(pipe, {"model__C": [0.01, 0.1, 1, 10]}, cv=5, scoring="roc_auc")
search.fit(X_train, y_train)
print("best C:", search.best_params_["model__C"], " CV ROC-AUC:", round(search.best_score_, 3))
best C: 0.1  CV ROC-AUC: 0.772

Slightly stronger regularization ($C = 0.1$, Lesson 10) helps a little.

Step 6 — Evaluate once on the test set

from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score, classification_report

best = search.best_estimator_
proba = best.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]
print("test ROC-AUC:", round(roc_auc_score(y_test, proba), 3))
print(classification_report(y_test, (proba >= 0.5).astype(int), target_names=["stayed", "churned"]))
test ROC-AUC: 0.765
              precision    recall  f1-score   support

      stayed       0.73      0.82      0.77       239
     churned       0.67      0.55      0.61       161

    accuracy                           0.71       400
   macro avg       0.70      0.68      0.69       400
weighted avg       0.71      0.71      0.70       400

Test ROC-AUC 0.765 is close to the cross-validated 0.772, so our estimate was honest. At the default threshold the model catches 55% of churners (recall) and is right 67% of the time when it flags someone (precision). If a retention offer is cheap, the company could lower the threshold to catch more churners at the cost of more false alarms (Lesson 9).

Step 7 — Interpret the model

names = best.named_steps["prep"].get_feature_names_out()
coefs = best.named_steps["model"].coef_[0]
for name, c in sorted(zip(names, coefs), key=lambda t: -abs(t[1]))[:5]:
    print(f"{name:32s} {c:+.2f}")
cat__contract_month-to-month     +0.85
num__tenure_months               -0.59
num__support_calls               +0.45
cat__contract_one-year           -0.43
cat__contract_two-year           -0.42

Because features were standardised, the coefficients are comparable (Lesson 6). Month-to-month contracts and more support calls push towards churn; longer tenure and annual contracts push away. These match the patterns built into the data — a good sanity check. Remember: these describe associations, not proven causes.

Step 8 — Save, reload and predict

import joblib

joblib.dump(best, "churn_model.joblib")
reloaded = joblib.load("churn_model.joblib")       # only ever load files you trust!

new_customer = pd.DataFrame([{"tenure_months": 3, "monthly_charge": 95.0, "support_calls": 4,
                              "contract": "month-to-month", "payment": "check", "city": "Pune",
                              "total_spent": 285.0}])
print("churn probability:", round(reloaded.predict_proba(new_customer)[0, 1], 3))
churn probability: 0.958

The whole pipeline — feature creation, imputation, scaling, encoding and model — is saved as one file. Raw customer data goes in, a probability comes out. A new, expensive, month-to-month customer with 4 support calls is flagged as very high risk.

One practical detail

The saved file stores a reference to the add_features function, not its code. To load the model in a different script or server, that function must be importable there too — for example, put it in a small module file (features.py) and import it in both places.

Security: loading model files

scikit-learn's documentation warns that pickle-based formats (pickle, joblib) can execute arbitrary code when loaded. Never load a model file from a source you don't trust. Safer formats include skops.io (which lets you inspect untrusted types before loading) and ONNX. Pickle-based files also need the same library versions that were used to save them.

10.After deployment: monitoring

A model's performance can quietly decay because the world changes (Lesson 5's distribution shift). Google's Rules of Machine Learning warns to "watch for silent failures" — for example, a feature that used to be filled in for 90% of rows dropping to 60% because an upstream system changed. In practice:

  • Log inputs and predictions; track the distribution of each feature and of the predicted probabilities over time.
  • When true outcomes arrive (did the customer actually leave?), keep measuring real-world metrics.
  • Check for training/serving skew: is production data processed exactly like training data?
  • Retrain regularly on recent data, and evaluate on data from later than the training period.

11.The complete ML workflow — a checklist

  1. Define the problem, the label and the metric that reflects real costs.
  2. Collect and explore the data: types, gaps, imbalance, oddities.
  3. Split off a test set immediately (by time, if the data is time-ordered).
  4. Build a pipeline: feature engineering, imputation, encoding, scaling.
  5. Score a trivial baseline.
  6. Compare several model families with cross-validation.
  7. Tune the best one or two.
  8. Evaluate once on the test set; choose a decision threshold.
  9. Interpret and sanity-check the model.
  10. Save the whole pipeline, deploy, and monitor.

12.Congratulations — and where to go next

You've gone from "what is a model?" to building, evaluating and saving complete machine learning systems — and you understand the maths underneath: vectors, gradients, probability, loss functions, regularization, and backpropagation. Ideas to explore next:

  • Practice on real datasets: the scikit-learn documentation's example gallery is full of complete, runnable examples.
  • Deep learning in depth: install PyTorch and build the CNN from Lesson 19; the free Deep Learning book by Goodfellow, Bengio and Courville goes much further.
  • Stronger maths: Mathematics for Machine Learning (Deisenroth, Faisal & Ong) is free online and builds directly on Lessons 2–4.
  • Revisit the demos: re-reading a lesson after the later ones often makes things click.

13.Running example: Chennai Homes

A complete pipeline: impute a missing age, scale the numbers, one-hot encode the area, then ridge regression. Adding the area feature didn't help here (MAE 6.9 → 7.2 lakh) — distance already carries most of that information, and with 12 houses every extra column adds noise.

Same 12 houses as Lesson 1. With so little data, treat the numbers as an illustration of the method, not as reliable estimates.

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
df = pd.read_csv("houses.csv")   # download it from Lesson 1
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler, OneHotEncoder
from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score
df.loc[3, "age_yrs"] = np.nan                     # pretend one value is missing
num = ["size_m2", "bedrooms", "dist_km", "age_yrs"]
numeric = Pipeline([("impute", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")), ("scale", StandardScaler())])
with_area = ColumnTransformer([("num", numeric, num), ("cat", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore"), ["area"])])
numbers_only = ColumnTransformer([("num", numeric, num)])
for name, prep in [("numbers only", numbers_only), ("numbers + area", with_area)]:
    model = Pipeline([("prep", prep), ("ridge", Ridge(alpha=1.0))])
    mae = -cross_val_score(model, df, df["price_lakh"], cv=4, scoring="neg_mean_absolute_error").mean()
    print(f"{name:15s} cross-validated MAE: {mae:.1f} lakh")

Output:

numbers only    cross-validated MAE: 6.9 lakh
numbers + area  cross-validated MAE: 7.2 lakh
Where this is used
  • Every real-world ML system: churn prediction, demand forecasting, risk scoring…

Choose it when: Always.

Misconceptions to unlearn

MythFeature engineering is obsolete now that we have deep learning.

RealityFor tabular data, good features and careful preprocessing are still among the biggest drivers of performance.

MythOnce a model is deployed, the work is done.

RealityData changes over time; models need monitoring and retraining.

Responsible AI · Responsible deployment

A model in production makes decisions at scale, so document it: model cards (Mitchell et al., 2019) record what the model is for, how it was evaluated, for which groups, and its known limits. Monitor for drift and for unequal error rates, watch for feedback loops (a model's decisions changing the data it later learns from), and make sure people affected can question a decision and reach a human.

14.Questions beginners often ask

How much time goes into data preparation?

In real projects, usually more than into modelling. Clean, well-understood data matters more than the choice of algorithm.

Should I always build new features?

Only if they add new information. Test each one with cross-validation — Exercise 4 in this lesson shows a feature that doesn't help.

What should I learn next?

Practise on real datasets end to end, then go deeper into whichever area interests you: deep learning, time series, or the maths.

Common mistakes to avoid
  • Fitting any preprocessing step on the full dataset before splitting.
  • Label-encoding unordered categories as 1, 2, 3 for linear or distance-based models.
  • Deploying without monitoring, so silent data changes go unnoticed.
Interview corner

Don't confuse

  • Normalisation vs standardisation — Squeeze into a range vs centre and scale.
  • One-hot vs label vs ordinal encoding — Switches, ID numbers, or ranks.
  • Data drift vs concept drift — New questions vs new answers to old questions.

Hidden questions — answer in your head first, then open.

Where should the mean and standard deviation for scaling come from?

The trap: "From the whole dataset."

From the training data only, then reused unchanged for validation, test and production data. Computing them on everything leaks information about the test set.

When you one-hot encode a category for linear regression, why drop one column?

The trap: Keeping all columns by habit.

With an intercept, the one-hot columns always sum to 1, the same as the intercept column — perfect collinearity (the "dummy variable trap"). Dropping one column fixes it. Regularised models and trees don't need this.

Why is target encoding risky, and how is it done safely?

The trap: Replacing each category with its average target on the full data.

Each row's own label contributes to its encoded value, so rare categories leak the answer and the model looks unrealistically good. Compute encodings out of fold (from other folds' data only) and add smoothing towards the overall mean.

You oversample the minority class (e.g. SMOTE), then split into train and test. What's wrong?

The trap: Thinking resampling is just preprocessing.

Synthetic or duplicated minority examples end up on both sides, inflating the test score. Resample the training data only, inside cross-validation, and evaluate on untouched, naturally imbalanced data.

All 8 hidden questions for this lesson →

15.Key takeaways

  • Good features often matter more than the choice of algorithm.
  • Scale numbers for distance/gradient models, log-transform skewed amounts, one-hot encode categories, and impute missing values (optionally with an indicator).
  • Create features from domain knowledge: ratios, date parts, aggregates.
  • Put everything in a Pipeline + ColumnTransformer so it's fitted on training data only and deployed as one object.
  • Workflow: split → baseline → compare with CV → tune → test once → interpret → save → monitor.

16.Check your understanding

1. Why not encode cities as Chennai = 1, Mumbai = 2, Delhi = 3 for a linear model?

Arbitrary numbers impose a fake order and spacing. One-hot encoding treats categories as equally different.

2. Where should the median used to fill missing values come from?

Like all learned preprocessing statistics, it must come from training data to avoid leakage.

3. A column holds account balances from 0 to 5,000,000, mostly under 10,000. A sensible transformation is…

The log compresses the huge range so a few extreme values don't dominate. log1p also handles zeros.

4. What is the main advantage of putting preprocessing inside a Pipeline?

Pipelines prevent leakage and guarantee identical processing in training and deployment.

5. Your new model scores ROC-AUC 0.52 and the baseline scores 0.50. What does that tell you?

Always compare with a baseline; a tiny improvement over random ranking means little useful signal has been captured.
