Exercise 1By hand

Training values of a feature are $10, 20, 30$. Standardise the new value 40 (divide by $n$).

Check your answer:

Show solution
$\mu = 20$, $\sigma = \sqrt{(100 + 0 + 100)/3} \approx 8.165$. $z = (40 - 20)/8.165 \approx 2.45$. Training statistics are reused — never recomputed on new data.
Exercise 2By hand

One-hot encode the sizes small, large, medium, small (categories in alphabetical order: large, medium, small).

Show solution
small → $(0, 0, 1)$; large → $(1, 0, 0)$; medium → $(0, 1, 0)$; small → $(0, 0, 1)$.
Exercise 3Concepts

What's wrong? X = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X), then train_test_split(X, y), then cross_val_score(model, X_train, y_train).

Show solution
The scaler was fitted on all data (including test rows) — leakage. Split first and put the scaler inside a Pipeline so it's re-fitted on each fold.
Exercise 4Project

Extend the churn project: add a feature is_new_customer (tenure ≤ 6 months) inside add_features, add it to the numeric list, and re-run Steps 4–6. Did it help?

Show solution
Add X["is_new_customer"] = (X["tenure_months"] <= 6).astype(int). Compare the cross-validated ROC-AUC with the earlier 0.771. When we ran it, logistic regression stayed at exactly 0.771 — no gain. Tenure is already a feature, and the new column only repeats part of it. A useful lesson: a new feature must add new information. Any change smaller than the ± spread (about 0.01) isn't a real improvement.

Lesson 21: Ethics & Fairness in Machine Learning

Where bias comes from, how to measure fairness per group, why the criteria conflict, and what to do about it.

By the end of this lesson you can

  • Name the main kinds of harm and the places where bias enters an ML system
  • Compute selection rate, TPR, FPR and precision for each group from confusion-matrix counts
  • Explain demographic parity, equal opportunity, equalised odds and predictive parity, and the four-fifths rule
  • Explain why the fairness criteria conflict when base rates differ, and choose mitigations
Before you start

This lesson builds on:

  • Lesson 5: Data, Features & Generalization — Always judge a model on data it hasn't seen: split into train / validation / test, or use k-fold cross-validation. Overfitting = low training error but high test error. Never let test data leak into training.
  • Lesson 8: Logistic Regression — Logistic regression outputs a probability $p = \sigma(\mathbf{w}\cdot\mathbf{x} + b)$, is trained with log loss, and classifies with a threshold (often 0.5), giving a straight decision boundary.
  • Lesson 9: Evaluating Models — Accuracy can mislead. Precision $= TP/(TP+FP)$, recall $= TP/(TP+FN)$, and F1 balances them. Moving the threshold trades one for the other; ROC-AUC summarises all thresholds.

Where this fits: Steps back from building models to ask who they affect. It reuses the confusion matrix from Lesson 9 and the threshold idea from Lesson 8 to measure and reduce unfairness.

1.Why fairness is a machine-learning problem

Imagine a bank that replaces its loan officers with a model trained on ten years of past decisions. The model is 88% accurate, fast and consistent. Is it fair? Accuracy alone can't tell you. If past officers turned down qualified applicants from one neighbourhood, the model has learned to do the same — automatically, at scale, and with an air of objectivity that makes it harder to challenge.

Machine learning finds patterns in data, and data records the world as it was, including its unfairness. A model doesn't need to be told anyone's ethnicity or gender to discriminate: other features — a postcode, a first name, a gap in employment — can act as proxies. This lesson gives you the vocabulary, the numbers and the habits to notice and reduce these problems.

The core idea

A model can be accurate on average while making very different kinds of mistakes for different groups of people. Fairness work means measuring those differences, deciding which ones matter for the situation, and acting on them — a job for people, informed by numbers.

2.What can go wrong: kinds of harm

  • Allocation harms: a resource or opportunity — a loan, a job interview, a medical referral — is withheld from some groups more than others.
  • Quality-of-service harms: the system simply works worse for some people, like face recognition or speech recognition with higher error rates for some groups.
  • Representation harms: outputs reinforce stereotypes or erase groups, such as image search or text generation that reproduces biased associations.
  • Privacy and autonomy harms: people are profiled, re-identified or manipulated using data they never agreed to share for that purpose.

3.Where bias comes from

Bias can enter at every step of the workflow you learned in Lesson 5:

  1. Historical bias: the world itself was unequal, so even a perfect record of it teaches the model those patterns (the Amazon hiring model, Lesson 1).
  2. Representation (sampling) bias: some groups are under-represented in the training data, so the model is less accurate for them.
  3. Measurement and label bias: the label is a proxy for what you care about. Using healthcare cost to stand for health need under-served Black patients (Obermeyer et al., 2019; Lesson 5).
  4. Aggregation bias: one model for everyone ignores real differences between groups — for example, a medical threshold that suits one population but not another.
  5. Evaluation bias: the test set or benchmark doesn't reflect the people the model will actually be used on.
  6. Deployment and feedback loops: the model's decisions change the future data. Police sent where a model predicts crime record more crime there, which "confirms" the prediction.

4.Measuring fairness with group metrics

Split your test set by group and compute the confusion matrix (Lesson 9) for each group separately. From those counts come the standard fairness measures:

MeasureFormula (per group)"Fair" means equal…Name of the criterion
Selection rate$\frac{TP + FP}{\text{all}}$share of people approvedDemographic parity
True-positive rate (recall)$\frac{TP}{TP + FN}$chance a qualified person is approvedEqual opportunity
TPR and false-positive rate$\frac{TP}{TP+FN}$ and $\frac{FP}{FP+TN}$both kinds of errorEqualised odds
Precision (PPV)$\frac{TP}{TP + FP}$how reliable an approval isPredictive parity

A common summary is the demographic-parity ratio: the lower selection rate divided by the higher one. In US employment law the "four-fifths rule" of thumb treats a ratio below 0.8 as evidence of possible adverse impact that needs explaining.

Worked example — one loan model, two groups

A bank tests its model on 100 applicants from each of two groups. In group A, 50 would repay; in group B, 20 would.

GroupTPFPFNTN
A4051045
B124876

Selection rate: A $= 45/100 = 0.45$; B $= 16/100 = 0.16$. Ratio $0.16/0.45 \approx 0.36$ — far below 0.8.

True-positive rate: A $= 40/50 = 0.80$; B $= 12/20 = 0.60$. A qualified applicant from B is approved less often.

False-positive rate: A $= 5/50 = 0.10$; B $= 4/80 = 0.05$.

Precision: A $= 40/45 \approx 0.89$; B $= 12/16 = 0.75$.

Accuracy: A $= 85/100 = 0.85$; B $= 88/100 = 0.88$ — the model is more accurate for group B even though it fails B's qualified applicants more often. Accuracy alone hides the problem.

Make sense of it

The situation: A bank's compliance officer audits the loan model before it goes live, comparing two groups of applicants.

What the result tells you: Group B is approved far less often (16% vs 45%), and qualified B applicants are approved less often (60% vs 80%) — yet B's accuracy is higher. Each metric answers a different fairness question.

What if…?

  • Lower group B's threshold so it approves 32 people (16 who would repay, 16 who wouldn't): selection 0.32 (ratio 0.71), TPR 0.80 (now equal to A), but FPR doubles to 0.20 and precision falls to 0.50.
  • A smaller audit: if group B had only 10 people, one applicant would move B's selection rate by 10 points. Small groups need confidence intervals before conclusions.

Why it matters in ML: Fairness metrics are the confusion matrix (Lesson 9) computed per group. Changing a threshold for one group moves all its metrics at once — the trade-offs are unavoidable, so decide which matters most with the people affected.

5.Try it: one threshold or two?

Two groups, A (half would repay) and B (one in five would repay), each get a score from the same model. Move the thresholds and watch the per-group rates. Try to make the selection rates equal; then try to make the true-positive rates equal; then notice what happens to precision and accuracy.

6.You can't have everything: the impossibility result

Why not just make every rate equal? Because, when the groups' base rates differ (here 50% vs 20%), it is mathematically impossible except for a perfect classifier. For any group, the four quantities are tied together by an identity (Chouldechova, 2017):

$$\text{FPR} = \frac{p}{1-p}\cdot\frac{1-\text{PPV}}{\text{PPV}}\cdot\text{TPR},$$

where $p$ is the group's base rate. If two groups have the same PPV and the same TPR but different $p$, their FPRs must differ.

Worked example — checking the identity

Group A: $p = 0.5$, PPV $= 40/45$, TPR $= 0.8$: $\ \frac{0.5}{0.5}\cdot\frac{5/45}{40/45}\cdot 0.8 = 1\times0.125\times0.8 = 0.10$ ✓ (the FPR we computed).

Group B: $p = 0.2$, PPV $= 0.75$, TPR $= 0.6$: $\ \frac{0.2}{0.8}\cdot\frac{0.25}{0.75}\cdot0.6 = 0.25\times0.333\times0.6 = 0.05$ ✓.

Now suppose we tuned group B to match A's PPV (0.889) and TPR (0.8). The identity forces B's FPR to be $0.25\times0.125\times0.8 = 0.025$ — no longer equal to A's 0.10. Equal precision and equal opportunity together rule out equal false-positive rates.

Make sense of it

The situation: A regulator asks: "Can't you just make every error rate equal for both groups?"

What the result tells you: The identity links FPR, precision, TPR and the base rate. Because the groups' base rates differ (50% vs 20%), fixing two of the rates forces the third apart.

What if…?

  • Insist B's FPR equals A's 0.10 while keeping TPR 0.8: B's precision must drop to 0.67 (vs A's 0.89).
  • If both groups had the same base rate, the factor $\frac{p}{1-p}$ would be the same and all three rates could match.

Why it matters in ML: This is why fairness is a choice, not a setting. The impossibility comes from the data's base rates, not from a bad algorithm.

So choosing a fairness criterion is a value judgement. In lending, a bank may care most that qualified applicants are treated alike (equal opportunity). In criminal justice, critics of the COMPAS risk score (ProPublica, 2016) focused on unequal false-positive rates, while its makers pointed to equal predictive value — and both were right about their own measure. Kleinberg, Mullainathan and Raghavan (2016) proved a closely related result for calibrated scores.

7.What you can do about it

  • Fix the data (before training): collect more data for under-represented groups, check that labels measure what you care about, remove or rethink proxy features, re-weight examples so groups count fairly.
  • Constrain the model (during training): add a fairness penalty or constraint to the loss, just as regularisation adds a penalty (Lesson 10). Libraries such as Fairlearn and AIF360 implement several methods.
  • Adjust decisions (after training): choose thresholds per group to equalise a chosen rate, as in the demo. This is effective but can be legally restricted, because it treats groups differently explicitly — get legal advice.
  • Change the system, not just the model: keep a human in the loop for consequential decisions, give people an explanation and a way to appeal, monitor outcomes after deployment, and be willing not to deploy.
"Fairness through unawareness" doesn't work

Deleting the protected attribute does not remove bias when other features are correlated with it — and it makes the bias harder to measure, because you can no longer compute group metrics. Most practitioners keep the attribute out of the model's inputs but use it for auditing.

8.Beyond fairness: privacy, transparency and accountability

  • Privacy: collect only the data you need, with consent. Models can leak training data (membership inference, Lesson 10); differential privacy adds carefully calibrated random noise during training so that no single person's record changes the result much.
  • Transparency: prefer interpretable models for high-stakes decisions, and explain outputs to the people affected. Document data with datasheets (Gebru et al.) and models with model cards (Mitchell et al., 2019).
  • Accountability: someone must be responsible for a model's decisions, and there must be a route to contest them. Laws such as the EU AI Act (see Recent developments) now require risk management, documentation and human oversight for high-risk uses such as hiring and credit.
  • Wider impact: energy use, effects on workers, and misuse (deepfakes, surveillance) are part of the responsibility too.

9.A practical checklist before you deploy

  1. Purpose: who is affected, what decision does the model inform, and is ML appropriate at all?
  2. Data: who is missing or under-represented? Is the label a fair proxy for the real goal?
  3. Metrics: compute the confusion matrix, selection rate, TPR, FPR and PPV for every relevant group — and the uncertainty when groups are small.
  4. Choose: decide with stakeholders which errors matter most here, and which fairness criterion you will hold the model to.
  5. Document: write a model card: intended use, evaluation by group, known limitations.
  6. Monitor: after deployment, track group metrics over time and watch for feedback loops; provide explanations and appeals.

10.In Python: a fairness report from scratch

Everything above is just the confusion matrix computed per group. Here is a small report on a synthetic loan dataset in which group B has a lower base rate:

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

# A synthetic loan dataset: two groups with different base rates of repayment
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 2000
group = rng.choice(["A", "B"], size=n, p=[0.6, 0.4])
base = np.where(group == "A", 0.5, 0.2)              # share who would repay
repay = (rng.random(n) < base).astype(int)
score = np.clip(0.5 + 0.25 * (repay - 0.5) * 2 + rng.normal(0, 0.18, n), 0, 1)  # model's score
df = pd.DataFrame({"group": group, "repay": repay, "score": score})

def group_report(df, threshold):
    d = df.assign(approve=(df["score"] >= threshold).astype(int))
    rows = {}
    for g, s in d.groupby("group"):
        tp = ((s.approve == 1) & (s.repay == 1)).sum(); fp = ((s.approve == 1) & (s.repay == 0)).sum()
        fn = ((s.approve == 0) & (s.repay == 1)).sum(); tn = ((s.approve == 0) & (s.repay == 0)).sum()
        rows[g] = {"selection rate": (tp + fp) / len(s), "TPR": tp / (tp + fn), "FPR": fp / (fp + tn), "PPV": tp / (tp + fp)}
    return pd.DataFrame(rows).T.round(3)

r = group_report(df, threshold=0.6)
print(r)
print("demographic-parity ratio:", round(r.loc["B", "selection rate"] / r.loc["A", "selection rate"], 3))
   selection rate    TPR    FPR    PPV
A           0.430  0.799  0.039  0.956
B           0.178  0.801  0.025  0.887
demographic-parity ratio: 0.414

Read it like a fairness auditor: with one shared threshold, qualified applicants are treated alike — the true-positive rates are both 0.80 (equal opportunity holds). But group B is approved far less often (ratio 0.41, well below 0.8) and an approval is less reliable for B (PPV 0.89 vs 0.96) — both consequences of B's lower base rate, exactly as the impossibility result predicts.

11.Running example: Chennai Homes

Does the Lesson 8 model treat areas differently? It only sees distance and age, never the area name — yet distance is a near-perfect proxy for area. Every Central house is flagged as a fast seller (4 of 4), including the one that didn't sell fast (FPR 1.00); elsewhere only 3 of 8 are flagged and none wrongly. With 4 and 8 houses these rates are extremely noisy — one house moves a rate by 25 points — which is itself a fairness lesson: small groups need far more data before you trust their numbers.

Same 12 houses as Lesson 1. With so little data, treat the numbers as an illustration of the method, not as reliable estimates.

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
df = pd.read_csv("houses.csv")   # download it from Lesson 1
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_predict
cols = ["dist_km", "age_yrs"]                 # the model never sees "area"
clf = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression())
df["pred"] = cross_val_predict(clf, df[cols], df["sold_fast"], cv=4)   # honest out-of-fold predictions
df["group"] = np.where(df["area"] == "Central", "Central", "Not central")
for g, s in df.groupby("group"):
    tp = ((s.pred == 1) & (s.sold_fast == 1)).sum(); fp = ((s.pred == 1) & (s.sold_fast == 0)).sum()
    pos, neg = (s.sold_fast == 1).sum(), (s.sold_fast == 0).sum()
    print(f"{g:12s} n={len(s):2d}  base rate {s.sold_fast.mean():.3f}  flagged {s.pred.mean():.3f}  "
          f"TPR {tp / pos:.2f}  FPR {fp / neg if neg else float('nan'):.2f}")

Output:

Central      n= 4  base rate 0.750  flagged 1.000  TPR 1.00  FPR 1.00
Not central  n= 8  base rate 0.375  flagged 0.375  TPR 1.00  FPR 0.00
Where this is used
  • Auditing credit, hiring, insurance and healthcare models before deployment
  • Model cards and impact assessments required by regulators
  • Monitoring deployed models for unequal error rates

Choose it when: Always, whenever a model's decisions affect people.

Misconceptions to unlearn

MythAlgorithms are objective because they are maths.

RealityThe maths is objective about the data it's given; the data, the label, the features and the threshold all carry human choices.

MythA model that's accurate overall is fair.

RealityOverall accuracy can hide very different error rates for different groups, as the worked example shows (88% accuracy for B, yet B's qualified applicants are approved less often).

MythWe can satisfy every fairness definition if we try hard enough.

RealityWhen base rates differ, it is mathematically impossible (except for a perfect model). You must choose which criterion matters most.

Responsible AI · Fairness is a process, not a number

No single metric certifies a model as fair. Fairness work means involving the people affected, documenting choices and their reasons, and keeping the ability to question, override and switch off the system. Metrics are evidence for that conversation, not a replacement for it.

12.Questions beginners often ask

If I remove gender and ethnicity from the data, is my model fair?

Not necessarily. Other features (postcode, school, first name) can act as proxies, and without the attribute you can no longer measure group differences. Keep it for auditing.

Which fairness metric is the right one?

There is no universal answer. Ask which mistake hurts people most in this situation: missing qualified people (compare TPR), wrongly flagging people (compare FPR), or unequal access overall (compare selection rates). Decide with the people affected.

Isn't the model just reflecting reality?

It reflects the data, which records past decisions and unequal access as well as reality. A model used to make future decisions can lock those patterns in, so 'it's in the data' is a reason to look closer, not a defence.

Are fairness rules the same everywhere?

No. Laws differ by country and by domain (lending, employment, housing). The four-fifths rule is a US guideline for employment, not a universal law. Get legal advice for real deployments.

Common mistakes to avoid
  • Reporting only overall accuracy and never splitting the metrics by group.
  • Treating a tiny subgroup's rates as precise — with a handful of people, one person changes the rate a lot.
  • Deleting the protected attribute and assuming the problem is solved.
  • Choosing a fairness metric without involving the people the decisions affect.
Interview corner

Don't confuse

  • Demographic parity vs equal opportunity vs equalised odds — Equal approvals, equal chances for the qualified, or equal errors of both kinds.
  • Disparate treatment vs disparate impact — Intent in the rule vs effect in the outcome.

Hidden questions — answer in your head first, then open.

If you remove gender and ethnicity from the data, is the model fair?

The trap: "Yes, it can't see them."

Not necessarily. Other features (postcode, school, first name) act as proxies, and without the attribute you can't even measure group differences. Keep it out of the inputs if appropriate, but use it for auditing.

Can a model have equal precision, equal TPR and equal FPR across two groups?

The trap: "Just tune the thresholds."

Not if the groups' base rates differ (unless the model is perfect). The identity $\text{FPR} = \frac{p}{1-p}\cdot\frac{1-\text{PPV}}{\text{PPV}}\cdot\text{TPR}$ forces at least one to differ. In Lesson 21's loan example, equalising FPR at 0.10 drops group B's precision to 0.67.

Group B's accuracy is higher than group A's. Does that show the model treats B fairly?

The trap: Using accuracy as the fairness measure.

No. In Lesson 21's example B had higher accuracy (0.88 vs 0.85) yet qualified B applicants were approved less often (TPR 0.60 vs 0.80). Compare the specific error rates that matter for the decision.

Is the four-fifths rule a law that defines fairness?

The trap: Treating it as universal.

It's a US employment-selection rule of thumb for spotting possible adverse impact, not a definition of fairness and not a law everywhere. Rules differ by country and domain.

All 5 hidden questions for this lesson →

13.Key takeaways

  • Models learn the unfairness in their data; proxies let them discriminate without seeing protected attributes.
  • Bias can enter through history, sampling, labels, aggregation, evaluation and feedback loops.
  • Fairness is measured by comparing per-group rates: selection rate (demographic parity), TPR (equal opportunity), TPR and FPR (equalised odds), precision (predictive parity).
  • When base rates differ, these criteria cannot all hold at once — choosing one is a value judgement to make with the people affected.
  • Mitigation happens in the data, the training, the thresholds and, above all, the surrounding system: documentation, human oversight, appeal and monitoring.
You've finished the course

That was the last lesson. To turn what you've learned into real skill, see What next: your learning plan — directions, a 12-week plan, project ideas and free resources.

14.Check your understanding

1. A model never receives applicants' ethnicity. Can it still discriminate by ethnicity?

Features like postcode or school are often correlated with protected attributes, so a model can reproduce group differences without the attribute itself.

2. Group A's selection rate is 0.50 and group B's is 0.30. What is the demographic-parity ratio, and does it pass the four-fifths rule of thumb?

$0.30/0.50 = 0.6$, which is below 0.8, so it would be flagged for possible adverse impact.

3. "Equal opportunity" asks which rate to be the same for every group?

Equal opportunity (Hardt, Price & Srebro, 2016) requires that qualified people — the true positives — are approved at the same rate in every group.

4. Two groups have different base rates. A model has equal precision and equal TPR for both. What must be true?

By the identity $\text{FPR} = \frac{p}{1-p}\cdot\frac{1-\text{PPV}}{\text{PPV}}\cdot\text{TPR}$, different base rates $p$ force different FPRs.

5. A hospital model predicts healthcare spending to decide who gets extra care. What kind of bias is the biggest risk?

This is the Obermeyer et al. (2019) case: groups with less access to care spend less at the same level of need, so the label understates their need.

Work each exercise on paper (or in the lesson notebook), type your answer into the box to check it, and open the solution to compare your working. Answers can be decimals (round to 3 places), fractions like 2/3 or percentages like 75%. Every answer has been checked with Python. For hands-on coding practice, the lesson notebook ends with two coding challenges: fill in one missing line and an automatic check tells you whether it's right.

Exercise 1By hand

Group A: 60 of 200 applicants approved. Group B: 30 of 150 approved. Compute both selection rates and the demographic-parity ratio. Does it pass the four-fifths rule of thumb?

Check your answers:

Show solution
A: $60/200 = 0.30$. B: $30/150 = 0.20$. Ratio $= 0.20/0.30 \approx 0.667$, below 0.8, so it would be flagged for possible adverse impact.
Exercise 2By hand

In group C, 40 people would repay a loan; the model approves 30 of them. Of the 60 who would not repay, it approves 6. Compute TPR, FPR and precision.

Check your answers:

Show solution
TPR $= 30/40 = 0.75$. FPR $= 6/60 = 0.10$. Precision $= 30/(30+6) = 30/36 \approx 0.833$.
Exercise 3By hand

A group has base rate $p = 0.25$, precision 0.8 and TPR 0.6. Use the identity $\text{FPR} = \frac{p}{1-p}\cdot\frac{1-\text{PPV}}{\text{PPV}}\cdot\text{TPR}$ to find its FPR.

Check your answer:

Show solution
$\frac{0.25}{0.75}\cdot\frac{0.2}{0.8}\cdot 0.6 = 0.3333\times0.25\times0.6 = 0.05$.
Exercise 4Concepts

A university admissions model is trained on past admissions decisions. List two ways bias could enter, and one check you would run before using it.

Show solution
Historical bias: past decisions may have favoured some schools or groups, and the model copies them. Measurement bias: 'admitted' is a proxy for 'would succeed'. Representation bias: some groups have few past applicants. Check: compute selection rate and TPR (using later student success as the outcome) per group, with uncertainty for small groups.
Exercise 5Project

Take the synthetic loan data from the Python section. Choose a separate threshold for group B so that its selection rate is within 0.8 of group A's. What happens to B's TPR, FPR and precision?

Show solution
Lowering B's threshold raises its selection rate; TPR and FPR both rise and precision falls. Equalising one rate moves the others — the trade-off from the impossibility result. The exact numbers depend on the threshold you pick.
